verses.text: The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach,
Until the day in which he was taken up, after that he through the Holy Ghost had given commandments unto the apostles whom he had chosen:
To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:
And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me.
For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.
When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?
And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judæa, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.
And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel;
Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.
Then returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day’ s journey.

And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.
These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.
And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples, and said, (the number of names together were about an hundred and twenty,)
Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus.
For he was numbered with us, and had obtained part of this ministry.
Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.
And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.
For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take.
Wherefore of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,
Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.
And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.
And they prayed, and said, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen,
That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place.
And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

chapters.summary: Luke opens a second volume for "Theophilus," recalling "all that Jesus began both to do and teach" until the day he was taken up. He had shown himself "alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days," speaking of "the things pertaining to the kingdom of God," and told them to stay in Jerusalem and "wait for the promise of the Father," since "ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence." Asked whether he will "at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel," he refuses the calendar—"It is not for you to know the times or the seasons"—and gives a map: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judæa, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." As they watch, "a cloud received him out of their sight," and two men "in white apparel" ask, "why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" promising he "shall so come in like manner." Returning from Olivet, the eleven are named; with "the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren" they continue "with one accord in prayer and supplication." Peter stands among about "an hundred and twenty," reads the defection of Judas as scripture fulfilled—"his bishoprick let another take"—and requires a replacement who companied with them from John's baptism and can "be a witness with us of his resurrection." The assembly prays to the Lord "which knowest the hearts of all men," casts lots, and Matthias is "numbered with the eleven apostles."
takeaways: The ascension is not Christ's disappearance but his enthronement; the same body seen for forty days is received into heaven and will return "in like manner," so Christian hope is fixed on a person rather than on an idea.
Jesus deliberately withholds the timetable and hands over a task, redirecting apocalyptic curiosity into witness that begins where the disciples stand and widens outward to the whole earth.
The Church begins by waiting and praying rather than organizing, and the promised Spirit—not the disciples' zeal—is the source of the power they are told to expect.

Apostolic ministry is described as an office that can be vacated and filled, chosen through prayer and the discernment of the whole assembly, with eyewitness of the resurrection as its defining qualification.

crossRefs.label: Luke 24:44-53 — the promise of the Father, and Jesus carried up into heaven
crossRefs.why: Luke closes his Gospel with the same commission to be witnesses, the same instruction to "tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high," and the ascension itself. Reading the two accounts together shows Acts deliberately picking up the thread where the Gospel laid it down.

crossRefs.label: Luke 1:1-4 — an orderly account written for most excellent Theophilus
crossRefs.why: Luke's Gospel opens by naming its recipient and grounding its report in those "which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word." The matching address to Theophilus marks Acts as the second half of one carefully researched work, so the standard of eyewitness testimony carries straight into the apostolic story.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 109:8 — let another take his office
crossRefs.why: The psalm prays that a treacherous accuser lose his days and that "another take his office." Peter applies it to the vacancy left by Judas, which is why the eleven treat the replacement as something Scripture requires rather than as a matter of their own preference.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 7:13-14 — one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven
crossRefs.why: Daniel sees a human figure carried on clouds into the presence of the Ancient of days and given "an everlasting dominion." The cloud that receives Jesus is not stage scenery but the language of enthronement, so the ascension reads as the moment that vision is fulfilled.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 1:20-23 — God set him at his own right hand and gave him to be the head over all things to the church
crossRefs.why: Paul describes the risen Christ seated above every power and given as head to the Church, "which is his body." It supplies the theological consequence of the scene in Acts: the disciples are not left leaderless when the cloud closes, because the one taken up now governs the community he leaves behind.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the filling of the place left by Judas—"his bishoprick let another take"—is read as showing that apostolic ministry is a transmissible office rather than a purely personal calling, which is why the Church understands bishops as successors of the apostles and treats ordination as the ordinary way that office passes on.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally treat the choice of Matthias as a one-time restoration of the Twelve before Pentecost, noting that the stated requirement is having accompanied Jesus "beginning from the baptism of John" and being able to witness to the resurrection, conditions no later generation could meet. On that reading the passage does not establish a repeatable succession so much as complete the foundational apostolic circle. Both traditions agree that the Church remains bound to the apostles' testimony and that its ministry is received rather than self-appointed.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the naming of "Mary the mother of Jesus" among those who "continued with one accord in prayer and supplication" as she awaits the Spirit with the apostles, seeing her maternal presence at the Church's beginning as of a piece with her presence at its Lord's beginning, and as warrant for asking her prayers alongside the praying community.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally observe that Luke lists Mary here without comment among the women and the brethren, and that the narrative gives her no distinct role in what follows, so they read the verse as evidence of her faithful discipleship rather than of any mediating office. Both traditions honor her as a woman of persevering prayer who waits on the promise with the rest of the Church, and both read her presence as a sign of continuity between the Gospel and the community Christ leaves behind.

verses.text: And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.
And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.
And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them.
And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
And they were all amazed and marvelled, saying one to another, Behold, are not all these which speak Galilæans?
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judæa, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia,
Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes,
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
And they were all amazed, and were in doubt, saying one to another, What meaneth this?
Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine.
But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and said unto them, Ye men of Judæa, and all ye that dwell at Jerusalem, be this known unto you, and hearken to my words:
For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day.
But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel;

And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams:
And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy:
And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke:
The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before that great and notable day of the Lord come:
And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.
Ye men of Israel, hear these words; Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved of God among you by miracles and wonders and signs, which God did by him in the midst of you, as ye yourselves also know:
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.
For David speaketh concerning him, I foresaw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved:
Therefore did my heart rejoice, and my tongue was glad; moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope:
Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
Thou hast made known to me the ways of life; thou shalt make me full of joy with thy countenance.
Men and brethren, let me freely speak unto you of the patriarch David, that he is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day.
Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;
He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.
This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses.
Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear.
For David is not ascended into the heavens: but he saith himself, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand,
Until I make thy foes thy footstool.
Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.
Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.
And with many other words did he testify and exhort, saying, Save yourselves from this untoward generation.
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
And fear came upon every soul: and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles.
And all that believed were together, and had all things common;
And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need.
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.

chapters.summary: "When the day of Pentecost was fully come," the disciples are "all with one accord in one place" and a sound "as of a rushing mighty wind" fills the house; "cloven tongues like as of fire" rest on each, and all are "filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Devout Jews "out of every nation under heaven" hear their own languages and are "confounded," asking "What meaneth this?" while others mock that they are "full of new wine." Peter, "standing up with the eleven," notes it is only "the third hour of the day" and declares, "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel": "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh." He turns to Jesus of Nazareth, "a man approved of God," "delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God" yet crucified "by wicked hands," whom God raised, "having loosed the pains of death." Since David "is both dead and buried," his words "thou wilt not leave my soul in hell" must speak of Christ. Exalted "by the right hand of God," Jesus has "shed forth this, which ye now see and hear," and is "both Lord and Christ." The hearers, "pricked in their heart," ask "what shall we do?" and Peter answers, "Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins." Three thousand are added, continuing "in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."
takeaways: Pentecost is presented as prophecy arriving rather than as religious enthusiasm: Peter's first move is not to describe the experience but to name the text it fulfils, so the Spirit's outpouring is measured against Scripture.

The Spirit is poured out on "all flesh"—sons and daughters, servants and handmaidens—so the gift is not the property of a caste, and the miracle serves comprehension, letting each hearer receive "the wonderful works of God" in his own tongue.
Peter holds together God's "determinate counsel and foreknowledge" and genuine human guilt in the crucifixion, refusing to let divine purpose excuse the deed or the deed defeat the purpose.

The response to the gospel is concrete and communal: repentance, baptism for the remission of sins, the gift of the Spirit, and a shared life of teaching, fellowship, bread, and prayer that draws others in daily.

crossRefs.label: Joel 2:28-32 — I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh
crossRefs.why: Joel promises an outpouring on sons and daughters, old and young, servants and handmaids, culminating in the assurance that "whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered." Peter quotes it as the interpretive key to the whole morning, so reading the prophet shows how much of the sermon is simply the text applied.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 16:8-11 — thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption
crossRefs.why: The psalm expresses confidence that God will not abandon his faithful one to the grave or to decay. Peter argues that David, whose "sepulchre is with us unto this day," cannot have spoken of himself, which turns the psalm into the earliest scriptural proof of the resurrection.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 11:1-9 — at Babel the LORD confounds the language of all the earth
crossRefs.why: At Babel a project of self-made greatness ends with speech confused and the builders scattered across the world. Pentecost gathers the scattered nations back and gives understanding instead of confusion, so the two scenes read as the undoing and the healing of the same wound.

crossRefs.label: Luke 3:15-17 — he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire
crossRefs.why: John the Baptist distinguishes his water baptism from the one to come, promising a baptism "with the Holy Ghost and with fire." The tongues of fire resting on each disciple are Luke's signal that the Baptist's promise, repeated by Jesus before the ascension, has now been kept.

crossRefs.label: Romans 10:9-13 — whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes the same line from Joel that closes Peter's citation and draws from it that "there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek." Read alongside Pentecost, it shows the multilingual crowd as the first enactment of a promise Paul will later push out to the nations.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Peter's answer—"Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost"—is read as describing what baptism actually accomplishes rather than what it merely pictures, and the extension of the promise "unto you, and to your children" is understood as consistent with baptizing infants into that same covenant grace.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters differ among themselves here: many read the sequence as putting repentance and faith first, with baptism as the sign and seal of a forgiveness already received, and some conclude that only those who can repent should be baptized. Others within the Protestant traditions baptize infants on much the same covenantal grounds, reading "and to your children" as Peter does. Both traditions agree that baptism is commanded by Christ, joined to repentance and the gift of the Spirit, and is the ordinary door into the Church.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats the summary that the believers "continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers" as the earliest sketch of the Church's ordered life, with the apostles' teaching, the eucharistic breaking of bread, and common prayer already forming the shape that Catholic liturgy preserves.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the verse as a description of how the first believers lived rather than a prescription of liturgical form, and many take "breaking of bread" to cover ordinary shared meals as well as the Lord's Supper, especially since the next lines speak of "breaking bread from house to house" with "gladness and singleness of heart." Both traditions agree that apostolic teaching, genuine fellowship, the table, and prayer are the marks of a healthy church, and that these four are meant to be held together rather than chosen among.

verses.text: Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
And a certain man lame from his mother’s womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple;
Who seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple asked an alms.
And Peter, fastening his eyes upon him with John, said, Look on us.
And he gave heed unto them, expecting to receive something of them.
Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.
And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength.
And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.
And all the people saw him walking and praising God:
And they knew that it was he which sat for alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with wonder and amazement at that which had happened unto him.
And as the lame man which was healed held Peter and John, all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering.
And when Peter saw it, he answered unto the people, Ye men of Israel, why marvel ye at this? or why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk?

The God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob, the God of our fathers, hath glorified his Son Jesus; whom ye delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate, when he was determined to let him go.
But ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you;
And killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses.
And his name through faith in his name hath made this man strong, whom ye see and know: yea, the faith which is by him hath given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.
And now, brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers.
But those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
And he shall send Jesus Christ, which before was preached unto you:
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
For Moses truly said unto the fathers, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you.
And it shall come to pass, that every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed from among the people.
Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days.
Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.
Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities.

chapters.summary: Peter and John go up to the temple "at the hour of prayer," and meet a man "lame from his mother’s womb" laid daily at the gate "which is called Beautiful" to beg. Peter fastens his eyes on him, says "Look on us," and answers, "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk." Peter lifts him by the right hand, "and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength," so he enters the temple "walking, and leaping, and praising God." The people recognize the beggar and run together in Solomon's porch "greatly wondering." Peter deflects them: "why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk?" The God "of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob" has glorified his Son Jesus, whom they "delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate"; they "denied the Holy One and the Just," and "killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead." Faith in that name has given the man "this perfect soundness." Granting that "through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers," and that the prophets foretold "that Christ should suffer," Peter urges, "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out," awaiting "the times of restitution of all things." He cites Moses' promised prophet and Abraham's covenant, "in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed."
takeaways: The apostles hand on what they have rather than what they lack; the poverty of "Silver and gold have I none" is not an obstacle to the gift but the setting that makes clear whose power is at work.
Peter refuses credit for the healing at once, insisting it came neither by "our own power or holiness," which sets the pattern for all ministry: the minister is instrument, never source.
Guilt is named plainly and then met with mercy—ignorance is acknowledged, the cross is shown to have been foretold, and the invitation is to repent and be converted rather than to despair.

The gospel is presented as the keeping of Israel's own promises, from the God of the patriarchs through Moses and Samuel and the prophets, so that the blessing reaches "all the kindreds of the earth" without cancelling the covenant it flows from.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 18:15-19 — the LORD will raise up a Prophet like unto Moses
crossRefs.why: Moses promises a prophet from among the people's own brethren to whom they must listen, with God requiring an account from anyone who will not hearken. Peter quotes it directly, so reading the original shows why he can present Jesus as the one Israel was already told to expect and obey.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 35:5-6 — then shall the lame man leap as an hart
crossRefs.why: Isaiah pictures the age of God's coming as one in which blind eyes open and "the lame man leap as an hart." The beggar entering the temple "walking, and leaping, and praising God" is Luke's quiet signal that the promised age has begun, which is exactly what Peter goes on to argue.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 22:16-18 — in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed
crossRefs.why: God swears to Abraham that through his seed blessing will reach every nation. Peter ends his sermon with this promise and applies it first to his own hearers, so the covenant with Abraham becomes the frame in which the resurrection is preached in Jerusalem.

crossRefs.label: Luke 24:25-27 — beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded the things concerning himself
crossRefs.why: On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus opens the Scriptures to show that Christ had to suffer before entering his glory. Peter's claim that God "before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer" reads as the apostles now doing publicly what Jesus first did for two disciples privately.

crossRefs.label: 2 Peter 3:9-13 — new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness
crossRefs.why: The letter explains delay as God's patience, "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance," and looks toward a renewed creation. It gives content to "the times of restitution of all things," showing that the repentance Peter urges is aimed at a future restoration and not only at personal relief.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the healing worked when Peter speaks "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth" and takes the man "by the right hand" illustrates the sacramental principle that Christ acts through human ministers and visible gestures, while Peter's disclaimer of "our own power or holiness" makes clear that the effect comes from Christ rather than from the worthiness of the one who ministers.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the sign as an authenticating miracle attached to the founding preaching of the gospel, noting that Luke credits the outcome to "his name through faith in his name" rather than to any power lodged in the apostle or in the gesture. On that reading the episode says more about the authority of the message than about a continuing instrumental role for ministers. Both traditions agree that Christ alone heals, that the apostle claims nothing for himself, and that the miracle exists to point hearers to the risen Lord.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading holds together Peter's call to "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out" with the expectation of "times of refreshing" and "the times of restitution of all things," understanding conversion as a real turning that begins now, is sustained through the Church's ministry of forgiveness, and is completed only in the final restoration of creation.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally emphasize that the blotting out of sins is God's free and immediate act received by repentant faith, complete from the moment a person turns to Christ, with the coming restoration as its public vindication rather than its completion. They read the verse as an evangelistic appeal rather than a description of an ongoing penitential process. Both traditions agree that repentance is genuinely required, that God alone blots out sin, and that the forgiveness given now looks forward to the renewal of all things.

verses.text: And as they spake unto the people, the priests, and the captain of the temple, and the Sadducees, came upon them,
Being grieved that they taught the people, and preached through Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
And they laid hands on them, and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide.
Howbeit many of them which heard the word believed; and the number of the men was about five thousand.
And it came to pass on the morrow, that their rulers, and elders, and scribes,
And Annas the high priest, and Caiaphas, and John, and Alexander, and as many as were of the kindred of the high priest, were gathered together at Jerusalem.
And when they had set them in the midst, they asked, By what power, or by what name, have ye done this?
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, said unto them, Ye rulers of the people, and elders of Israel,
If we this day be examined of the good deed done to the impotent man, by what means he is made whole;

Be it known unto you all, and to all the people of Israel, that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom ye crucified, whom God raised from the dead, even by him doth this man stand here before you whole.
This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner.
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
And beholding the man which was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it.
But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves,
Saying, What shall we do to these men? for that indeed a notable miracle hath been done by them is manifest to all them that dwell in Jerusalem; and we can not deny it.
But that it spread no further among the people, let us straitly threaten them, that they speak henceforth to no man in this name.
And they called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
For we can not but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
So when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding nothing how they might punish them, because of the people: for all men glorified God for that which was done.
For the man was above forty years old, on whom this miracle of healing was shewed.
And being let go, they went to their own company, and reported all that the chief priests and elders had said unto them.
And when they heard that, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, Lord, thou art God, which hast made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all that in them is:
Who by the mouth of thy servant David hast said, Why did the heathen rage, and the people imagine vain things?
The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord, and against his Christ.
For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together,
For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.
And now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word,
By stretching forth thine hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done by the name of thy holy child Jesus.
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
And with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus: and great grace was upon them all.
Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,
And laid them down at the apostles’ feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need.
And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, ( which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus,
Having land, sold it, and brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

chapters.summary: As they speak, the priests, "the captain of the temple," and the Sadducees arrive, "being grieved that they taught the people, and preached through Jesus the resurrection from the dead," and hold them overnight; yet "many of them which heard the word believed," numbering about five thousand. Next morning the council, with Annas and Caiaphas, asks, "By what power, or by what name, have ye done this?" Peter, "filled with the Holy Ghost," answers that the man stands whole "by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom ye crucified, whom God raised from the dead," and applies the psalm: "This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner." He concludes, "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." The council marvels at the boldness of "unlearned and ignorant men," recognizes "that they had been with Jesus," and with the healed man standing there "could say nothing against it." They order them "not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus," and hear the reply, "we can not but speak the things which we have seen and heard." Released, the company prays, quoting "Why did the heathen rage," and asking not for safety but that "with all boldness they may speak thy word." The place is shaken, all are "filled with the Holy Ghost," and the believers, "of one heart and of one soul," hold all things common.
takeaways: The first opposition to the Church is provoked by the resurrection, not by ethics: what the authorities cannot tolerate is the claim that the crucified man is alive, which is precisely the claim the apostles refuse to soften.

Peter's "none other name" is exclusive about the source of salvation rather than boastful about the speakers; the same sentence that narrows salvation to Christ has just described him as the stone rejected by those now judging the case.

Conscience before God outranks lawful human authority when the two conflict, and the apostles state this without contempt, inviting the council itself to "judge ye" whether obeying men over God could be right.

The believers pray for courage rather than deliverance, and the Spirit's answer shows itself both in bold speech and in a shared life where, as Luke records, "Neither was there any among them that lacked."

crossRefs.label: Psalm 118:22-23 — the stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner
crossRefs.why: The psalm celebrates a rejected stone that God makes the cornerstone, calling it "the LORD’s doing." Peter quotes it to the very builders he has in view, turning the trial into an argument that God has already reversed their verdict on Jesus.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 2:1-3 — why do the heathen rage, and the rulers take counsel together against the LORD
crossRefs.why: The psalm pictures nations and rulers conspiring against God and his anointed, and being unable to prevail. The praying community quotes it after their release, which lets them read the threats of a powerful council as something Scripture had already anticipated and God had already answered.

crossRefs.label: Luke 12:11-12 — the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say
crossRefs.why: Jesus tells the disciples not to rehearse a defence when brought before magistrates and powers, because the Spirit will supply the words. Luke's note that Peter spoke "filled with the Holy Ghost" before the council shows the promise being kept in the very setting it was made for.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 2:4-8 — a living stone, disallowed of men, but chosen of God, and precious
crossRefs.why: The letter develops the same cornerstone imagery Peter uses at his trial, adding that believers are built as "lively stones" into a spiritual house. Read together, the courtroom argument becomes a whole ecclesiology: the rejected stone gathers a people around itself.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 8:13-15 — by an equality, that your abundance may be a supply for their want
crossRefs.why: Paul organizes a collection so that surplus in one church meets need in another, quoting the manna rule that the one who gathered much had nothing over. It shows the Jerusalem practice of holding all things common developing into an ongoing habit of sharing across distances rather than remaining a single memorable episode.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Peter's declaration that "there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" is held firmly as meaning that whoever is saved is saved by Christ alone, while the same tradition also teaches that his saving grace can reach people who through no fault of their own never hear the gospel preached, so that the exclusivity belongs to Christ rather than to the extent of human knowledge of him.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the verse in the context of Peter's preaching to hearers who have just been told to repent, and many conclude that it requires explicit faith in the name that has been announced, which lends the missionary task its urgency. Some Protestant readers allow more room for God's mercy toward the unevangelized, but the emphasis usually falls on the necessity of hearing and believing. Both traditions agree without qualification that salvation is found in Christ and in no other name, and that the Church is obliged to make that name known.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the picture of believers "of one heart and of one soul" who laid the proceeds of sold property "down at the apostles’ feet" for distribution as more than an anecdote, seeing in it a foundation for consecrated common life and for the conviction that private ownership carries a duty toward the needy, with the apostolic ministry entrusted to oversee the sharing.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the sharing as spontaneous and voluntary rather than as a required structure, pointing to Peter's later words to Ananias about the unsold land, "was it not thine own?", as evidence that no one was compelled to sell. On that reading Luke describes the fruit of grace in a particular community rather than prescribing an economic order for the Church. Both traditions agree that the Spirit produces concrete material care so that no believer is left in want, and that generosity of this kind is a mark of genuine faith.

verses.text: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession,
And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land?
Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost: and great fear came on all them that heard these things.
And the young men arose, wound him up, and carried him out, and buried him.
And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in.
And Peter answered unto her, Tell me whether ye sold the land for so much? And she said, Yea, for so much.
Then Peter said unto her, How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? behold, the feet of them which have buried thy husband are at the door, and shall carry thee out.
Then fell she down straightway at his feet, and yielded up the ghost: and the young men came in, and found her dead, and, carrying her forth, buried her by her husband.
And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.
And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; ( and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.
And of the rest durst no man join himself to them: but the people magnified them.
And believers were the more added to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women.)
Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them.
There came also a multitude out of the cities round about unto Jerusalem, bringing sick folks, and them which were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed every one.
Then the high priest rose up, and all they that were with him, (which is the sect of the Sadducees,) and were filled with indignation,
And laid their hands on the apostles, and put them in the common prison.
But the angel of the Lord by night opened the prison doors, and brought them forth, and said,
Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.

And when they heard that, they entered into the temple early in the morning, and taught. But the high priest came, and they that were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
But when the officers came, and found them not in the prison, they returned, and told,
Saying, The prison truly found we shut with all safety, and the keepers standing without before the doors: but when we had opened, we found no man within.
Now when the high priest and the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these things, they doubted of them whereunto this would grow.
Then came one and told them, saying, Behold, the men whom ye put in prison are standing in the temple, and teaching the people.
Then went the captain with the officers, and brought them without violence: for they feared the people, lest they should have been stoned.
And when they had brought them, they set them before the council: and the high priest asked them,
Saying, Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name? and, behold, ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.
Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.
And we are his witnesses of these things; and so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him.
When they heard that, they were cut to the heart, and took counsel to slay them.
Then stood there up one in the council, a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and commanded to put the apostles forth a little space;
And said unto them, Ye men of Israel, take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do as touching these men.

For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought.
After this man rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed.
And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:
But if it be of God, ye can not overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
And to him they agreed: and when they had called the apostles, and beaten them, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name.
And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.

chapters.summary: Ananias and Sapphira sell a possession but keep "back part of the price," bringing the rest as the whole. Peter asks, "why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost," reminding him that the land and its proceeds were freely his—"was it not thine own?"—and concludes, "thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God." Ananias falls and dies; three hours later his wife repeats the lie and is asked, "How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?" She too falls, and "great fear came upon all the church." Signs and wonders follow in Solomon's porch; the sick are laid in the streets so that "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them," while crowds from surrounding cities are "healed every one." The high priest and the Sadducees, "filled with indignation," jail the apostles, but an angel opens the doors by night: "Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life." Officers find the prison "shut with all safety" yet empty, and the apostles teaching openly. Charged with filling Jerusalem with their doctrine, Peter answers, "We ought to obey God rather than men," preaching Jesus exalted "to be a Prince and a Saviour." The council is "cut to the heart" until Gamaliel counsels restraint: "if it be of God, ye can not overthrow it." Beaten and forbidden the name, the apostles leave "rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name."
takeaways: The sin of Ananias is not withholding but pretending; Peter states plainly that the property was his to keep, so what destroys him is the staged appearance of a generosity he had not given.

Deceit inside the community is treated as deceit toward God, because the Spirit who fills the Church is genuinely present in it, which makes hypocrisy in the assembly a matter of far more weight than mere reputation.

Obedience to God above human authority is stated as a principle, but the apostles pay for it rather than escape it: they are beaten and released, and they treat the shame as an honour to be received with joy.

Gamaliel's counsel—that a work of men collapses and a work of God cannot be overthrown—frames the whole conflict, and Luke lets the outcome answer the question by showing the apostles preaching daily and undeterred.

crossRefs.label: Joshua 7 — Achan takes of the accursed thing and hides it among his own stuff
crossRefs.why: Israel's first advance into the land stalls because one man secretly keeps for himself what had been devoted, and the concealed theft is treated as a sin of the whole people. The parallel at the Church's first advance shows Luke presenting Ananias not as an isolated fraud but as a danger to the community's integrity at its beginning.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 10:1-3 — Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire and die before the LORD
crossRefs.why: On the first day of ordered worship two priests improvise before God and are struck down, with the reason given as "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me." It supplies the pattern for a sudden judgment at the opening of something holy, which is how the deaths in Acts have long been read.

crossRefs.label: Luke 12:1-3 — beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy
crossRefs.why: Jesus warns that hypocrisy spreads like leaven and that "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed." The scene with Ananias and Sapphira is that warning made visible inside the Church itself, where a concealed arrangement is exposed within hours.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 11:27-32 — for this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep
crossRefs.why: Paul links unworthy participation in the Lord's Supper with real bodily consequences in the congregation, adding that "when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord." It offers the closest apostolic parallel to Acts 5, and reads such judgment as corrective discipline rather than final condemnation.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 4:12-16 — if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed
crossRefs.why: The letter tells believers not to be surprised by a fiery trial but to rejoice as partakers of Christ's sufferings, and to glorify God rather than feel disgrace. It is the settled teaching of the same Peter who walks away from a public beating "rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name."

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are read as showing that the Church is a genuinely holy communion in which the Spirit dwells, so that deceiving the assembly is deceiving God, and the passage has long been taken as an early warrant for the Church's authority to judge and exclude grave and unrepented sin from its common life.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the episode as an extraordinary act of God at the founding moment of the Church, a solemn warning against hypocrisy rather than a precedent for human authorities to impose penalties, noting that Peter announces the judgment but does not carry it out. They stress that the sentence falls from God directly and is never repeated in the narrative. Both traditions agree that the sin lay in lying to the Holy Ghost, and that the Spirit's real presence makes the community's honesty a serious matter rather than a formality.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in the crowds who hope that "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them" a scriptural precedent for the veneration of relics and for sacramentals, on the principle that God freely chooses to work through material things joined to holy persons rather than through invisible means alone.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally treat this as one of the extraordinary signs marking the apostolic age and authenticating the message, and they observe that Luke reports what the people expected without endorsing a practice or crediting the shadow itself. Many caution that inferring holy objects from the account goes beyond what the text states. Both traditions agree that God alone is the healer, that the apostles consistently refuse credit for such works, and that the signs exist to draw people toward Christ.

verses.text: And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.

And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch:
Whom they set before the apostles: and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.
And the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly; and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.
And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people.
Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen.
And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake.
Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God.
And they stirred up the people, and the elders, and the scribes, and came upon him, and caught him, and brought him to the council,
And set up false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law:
For we have heard him say, that this Jesus of Nazareth shall destroy this place, and shall change the customs which Moses delivered us.
And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.

chapters.summary: As "the number of the disciples was multiplied," "there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration." The twelve call the multitude together: "It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables." They tell the brethren to "look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom," while they themselves "give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word." The saying "pleased the whole multitude," and seven are chosen: Stephen, "a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost," with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, "a proselyte of Antioch." Set before the apostles, "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." Then "the word of God increased," and "a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith." Stephen, "full of faith and power," does "great wonders and miracles among the people," and men of a synagogue of "the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians" dispute with him, but "they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake." So they suborn men to charge him with "blasphemous words against Moses, and against God," and bring him before the council, where witnesses allege he speaks against "this holy place, and the law" and says Jesus "shall change the customs which Moses delivered us." All in the council see "his face as it had been the face of an angel."
takeaways: The Church's first recorded internal crisis is a failure of charity toward widows, and it is resolved not by silencing the complaint but by restructuring the community so that both the care of the poor and the preaching of the word receive dedicated ministers.

Apostolic ministry is shared without being surrendered: the twelve keep prayer and the word as their irreducible charge and hand on a genuine office to others through prayer and the laying on of hands, so the new ministry is derived from theirs rather than invented alongside it.

The seven are not merely administrators. They must be "full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom," and Stephen immediately preaches and works wonders, showing that serving tables and bearing witness to Christ belong to a single calling.

Opposition shifts from argument to accusation once "they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake." The charges brought against Stephen echo those brought against Jesus, and his face like an angel's signals whose Spirit is actually speaking.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 18:17-23 — Moses is counselled to appoint able men to share the burden
crossRefs.why: Jethro warns Moses that he will wear himself away judging alone and tells him to provide "able men, such as fear God" who will bear the burden with him. The apostles do the same thing under a new covenant, keeping the greater charge and delegating the rest to men chosen for character.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 11:16-17 — seventy elders receive of the spirit that rested on Moses
crossRefs.why: God tells Moses to gather seventy elders, promising, "I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them." It reads as the older pattern behind Acts 6, where authority is extended to others by God's own Spirit and not merely by administrative arrangement.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 3:8-13 — the qualities required of deacons
crossRefs.why: The letter lists what deacons must be, "grave, not doubletongued," holding "the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience," and promises them "a good degree" for serving well. By the time the letter is written the office is settled and named, which is why Acts 6 is so often read as its beginning.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 4:14 — the gift given with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery
crossRefs.why: Timothy is told, "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery," treating the imposition of hands as the occasion of a real and abiding gift. Read alongside Acts 6:6 it supports the understanding that the gesture confers something rather than merely announcing a decision.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 26:59-61 — the council seeks witnesses that Jesus threatened the temple
crossRefs.why: At Jesus' trial witnesses claim he said, "I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days." The accusation brought against Stephen, that Jesus "shall destroy this place," repeats the charge against the master, so the disciple's trial is deliberately shaped like the Lord's.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the setting of the seven before the apostles, followed by prayer and the laying on of hands, is read as the institution of the diaconate and as the earliest narrative of ordination, in which a permanent ministry is conferred by the apostles rather than a temporary task assigned.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally observe that the text never calls the seven deacons and describes a practical solution to a specific problem of food distribution, so they read the laying on of hands as the congregation's commissioning and blessing of chosen servants rather than the conferral of sacramental office. Many also note that Stephen and Philip promptly preach and baptize, which suggests their work was not confined to a fixed order at all. Both traditions agree that the Church rightly sets apart particular people for particular service, that character and the Holy Spirit are prerequisites, and that this is done through the prayer and hands of those already entrusted with authority.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the fact that the apostles themselves determine the shape of the new ministry, define its scope, and confer it, taking this as evidence that the Church under apostolic authority can establish and adapt offices as needs arise rather than being limited to structures already spelled out in Scripture.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally emphasize that the whole multitude selects the seven and that the apostles act on a need the congregation itself raised, reading the passage as a model of local church responsibility exercised under apostolic teaching rather than as a warrant for developing offices independent of the biblical pattern. They also stress the stated rationale, that nothing should displace prayer and the ministry of the word. Both traditions agree that the arrangement existed to serve the preaching of the gospel and the care of the poor, and that it was validated by the growth that immediately followed.

verses.text: Then said the high priest, Are these things so?
And he said, Men, brethren, and fathers, hearken; The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran,
And said unto him, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall shew thee.
Then came he out of the land of the Chaldæans, and dwelt in Charran: and from thence, when his father was dead, he removed him into this land, wherein ye now dwell.
And he gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on: yet he promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, when as yet he had no child.
And God spake on this wise, That his seed should sojourn in a strange land; and that they should bring them into bondage, and entreat them evil four hundred years.
And the nation to whom they shall be in bondage will I judge, said God: and after that shall they come forth, and serve me in this place.
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision: and so Abraham begat Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat the twelve patriarchs.
And the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: but God was with him,
And delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governor over Egypt and all his house.
Now there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance.
But when Jacob heard that there was corn in Egypt, he sent out our fathers first.
And at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren; and Joseph’s kindred was made known unto Pharaoh.
Then sent Joseph, and called his father Jacob to him, and all his kindred, threescore and fifteen souls.
So Jacob went down into Egypt, and died, he, and our fathers,
And were carried over into Sychem, and laid in the sepulchre that Abraham bought for a sum of money of the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem.
But when the time of the promise drew nigh, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
Till another king arose, which knew not Joseph.
The same dealt subtilly with our kindred, and evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children, to the end they might not live.
In which time Moses was born, and was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father’s house three months:
And when he was cast out, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son.
And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.
And when he was full forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel.
And seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and avenged him that was oppressed, and smote the Egyptian:
For he supposed his brethren would have understood how that God by his hand would deliver them: but they understood not.
And the next day he shewed himself unto them as they strove, and would have set them at one again, saying, Sirs, ye are brethren; why do ye wrong one to another?
But he that did his neighbour wrong thrust him away, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?
Wilt thou kill me, as thou diddest the Egyptian yesterday?
Then fled Moses at this saying, and was a stranger in the land of Madian, where he begat two sons.
And when forty years were expired, there appeared to him in the wilderness of mount Sina an angel of the Lord in a flame of fire in a bush.
When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight: and as he drew near to behold it, the voice of the Lord came unto him,
Saying, I am the God of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Then Moses trembled, and durst not behold.
Then said the Lord to him, Put off thy shoes from thy feet: for the place where thou standest is holy ground.
I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and am come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send thee into Egypt.
This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.
He brought them out, after that he had shewed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea, and in the wilderness forty years.
This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear.
This is he, that was in the church in the wilderness with the angel which spake to him in the mount Sina, and with our fathers: who received the lively oracles to give unto us:
To whom our fathers would not obey, but thrust him from them, and in their hearts turned back again into Egypt,
Saying unto Aaron, Make us gods to go before us: for as for this Moses, which brought us out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.
And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice unto the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.

Then God turned, and gave them up to worship the host of heaven; as it is written in the book of the prophets, O ye house of Israel, have ye offered to me slain beasts and sacrifices by the space of forty years in the wilderness?
Yea, ye took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan, figures which ye made to worship them: and I will carry you away beyond Babylon.
Our fathers had the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness, as he had appointed, speaking unto Moses, that he should make it according to the fashion that he had seen.
Which also our fathers that came after brought in with Jesus into the possession of the Gentiles, whom God drave out before the face of our fathers, unto the days of David;
Who found favour before God, and desired to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.
But Solomon built him an house.
Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet,
Heaven is my throne, and earth is my foot stool: what house will ye build me? saith the Lord: or what is the place of my rest?
Hath not my hand made all these things?
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One; of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers:
Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it.
When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.
But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
And said, Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God.
Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord,
And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul.
And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

chapters.summary: Asked, "Are these things so?", Stephen answers with Israel's whole story. "The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham" and said, "Get thee out of thy country," yet God "gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on" — only a promise. The patriarchs, "moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: but God was with him," and famine brought Jacob's household down to die there. Then a king "which knew not Joseph" oppressed them. Moses, "learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians," struck an Egyptian, supposing that God "by his hand would deliver them: but they understood not." Refused with "Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?", he fled; forty years later God spoke from the bush, "the place where thou standest is holy ground." "This Moses whom they refused" God sent as "a ruler and a deliverer," who foretold, "A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me" — yet the fathers "would not obey," made a calf, and "rejoiced in the works of their own hands." From tabernacle to temple he insists "the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands," then charges his hearers, "ye do always resist the Holy Ghost." They are "cut to the heart," cast him out and stone him, the witnesses laying their clothes at Saul's feet, while Stephen sees "the Son of man standing on the right hand of God" and dies praying, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge."
takeaways: Stephen's defense is a claim about how God works rather than a denial of the law: the promise runs ahead of the land, the tabernacle, and the temple, so God's presence is never held captive by a place, and "the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands."

The rejected deliverer is the recurring pattern of salvation history. Joseph sold by his brothers and Moses turned away with "Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?" are both sent back by God as saviors, preparing the hearer to recognize the crucified Jesus as "the Just One."

Resisting the Holy Ghost is presented as a standing temptation for God's own people, not the failing of one generation. Stephen speaks throughout of "our fathers" and stands inside the covenant he is calling his hearers to keep.

Christian martyrdom is measured by conformity to Christ. Stephen sees the Son of man standing to receive him, commits his spirit to Jesus, and forgives his killers, so that the witness dies as the Lord died and the story of Saul begins at his feet.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 12:1-5 — the call of Abram out of his country
crossRefs.why: The LORD tells Abram, "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee," and Abram goes with nothing but the promise. Stephen begins here on purpose, since the founding act of Israel is obedience to a God who calls people out of settled ground.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 3:2-10 — the burning bush and the holy ground
crossRefs.why: God speaks from the bush, "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground," and says, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt." Stephen retells this to show that holy ground appeared in a wilderness far from any sanctuary, which is the point his accusers most need to hear.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 18:15-19 — the LORD will raise up a Prophet like unto Moses
crossRefs.why: Moses promises, "The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken." Stephen quotes this as the hinge of his argument: honoring Moses means listening to the prophet Moses foretold, so the charge of speaking against Moses collapses.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 66:1-2 — heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool
crossRefs.why: The prophet asks, "where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?" and says God looks instead to the one "that is poor and of a contrite spirit." Stephen quotes it almost exactly, so his critique of temple confidence is not innovation but the prophets' own voice.

crossRefs.label: Luke 23:34-46 — Jesus forgives his executioners and commends his spirit
crossRefs.why: On the cross Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do," and finally, "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Stephen's two dying prayers deliberately mirror both, with the difference that he addresses them to Jesus, which is itself a confession of who Jesus is.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Stephen's dying words, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit," are read as prayer addressed directly to the risen Christ and as evidence that the martyr is received into glory at once, which underlies the Church's practice of honoring the martyrs, keeping their memory in her worship, and asking their prayers.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the same words primarily as a confession of Christ's divinity and of personal trust at the hour of death, since Stephen prays to Jesus what Jesus prayed to the Father. Many hold that honoring the martyrs by imitating their courage is one thing, while addressing prayer to them is another, and they prefer to keep the focus on the Christ who stands to receive him. Both traditions agree that Stephen dies in living communion with the Lord, that his death is a genuine victory rather than a defeat, and that the Church rightly remembers him.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands" as a warning against confining God to a building rather than a rejection of sacred space, holy places, or ordered public worship, since the temple's meaning is understood to be fulfilled in Christ and carried forward in the Church's sacramental worship rather than simply abolished.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally hear a stronger note of discontinuity, reading Stephen as announcing that temple-centered religion has reached its end and that God now dwells in his people, which is why the speech was heard as such a threat. On this reading the emphasis falls on the gathered believers as God's dwelling rather than on any consecrated location. Both traditions agree that God is not contained or controlled by any structure, that Solomon's house was never meant to house him, and that Christ himself is where God and his people meet.
