verses.text: And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judæa and Samaria, except the apostles.
And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.
As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison.
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them.
And the people with one accord gave heed unto those things which Philip spake, hearing and seeing the miracles which he did.
For unclean spirits, crying with loud voice, came out of many that were possessed with them: and many taken with palsies, and that were lame, were healed.
And there was great joy in that city.
But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one:
To whom they all gave heed, from the least to the greatest, saying, This man is the great power of God.
And to him they had regard, because that of long time he had bewitched them with sorceries.
But when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip, and wondered, beholding the miracles and signs which were done.
Now when the apostles which were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John:
Who, when they were come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Ghost:
( For as yet he was fallen upon none of them: only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.)
Then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost.
And when Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles’ hands the Holy Ghost was given, he offered them money,
Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost.
But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.
Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God.
Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee.
For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.
Then answered Simon, and said, Pray ye to the Lord for me, that none of these things which ye have spoken come upon me.
And they, when they had testified and preached the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans.
And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert.

And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,
Was returning, and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet.
Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot.
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him.
The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth:
In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth.
And the eunuch answered Philip, and said, I pray thee, of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?
Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?
And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.
And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip was found at Azotus: and passing through he preached in all the cities, till he came to Cæsarea.

chapters.summary: "And Saul was consenting unto his death." Persecution scatters the Jerusalem church "throughout the regions of Judæa and Samaria, except the apostles," and Saul "made havock of the church"; yet "they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word." Philip goes down to Samaria and "preached Christ unto them," with healings and exorcisms, and "there was great joy in that city." Simon, a sorcerer the people had called "the great power of God," believes and is baptized. When the apostles hear "that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John," who pray for them, "For as yet he was fallen upon none of them: only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus"; then "laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Simon offers money for the power; Peter answers, "Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money," telling him to repent, for "thou art in the gall of bitterness." An angel then sends Philip toward Gaza, where an Ethiopian eunuch sits reading Isaiah. Asked, "Understandest thou what thou readest?", he answers, "How can I, except some man should guide me?" Philip "began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus." Seeing water, the eunuch asks, "what doth hinder me to be baptized?", confesses, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God," is baptized, and "went on his way rejoicing," while Philip is found at Azotus, preaching to Cæsarea.
takeaways: Persecution does not shrink the Church but disperses it. The mission to Samaria begins because believers were driven from home, and what looks like the loss of a settled center becomes the next stage of the gospel's advance.

Baptism and the gift of the Spirit are shown here as distinguishable moments. The Samaritans are genuinely baptized "in the name of the Lord Jesus," and the Spirit is given afterward through the prayer and hands of apostles sent from Jerusalem, binding the new believers to the one apostolic body.

Simon names a permanent temptation: treating God's gifts as a commodity or as leverage over others. Peter locates the fault in the man rather than only in the offer, "thy heart is not right in the sight of God," and calls him to repentance rather than simply dismissing him.

The eunuch is already reading the prophet and still asks, "How can I, except some man should guide me?" The word reaches him through someone sent, and the encounter ends not in understanding alone but in confession, baptism, and joy.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 53:7-8 — the servant led as a lamb to the slaughter
crossRefs.why: This is the passage the eunuch was reading, of one who "opened not his mouth" and "was cut off out of the land of the living." Reading it whole shows why Philip could begin at that scripture and preach Jesus without changing the subject.

crossRefs.label: John 4:20-26 — Jesus and the Samaritan woman on where God is worshipped
crossRefs.why: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father," while still saying "salvation is of the Jews." The Samaritan mission in Acts 8 is the promised hour arriving, with the old division healed rather than merely ignored.

crossRefs.label: Acts 19:1-6 — disciples at Ephesus are baptized and then receive the Spirit through Paul's hands
crossRefs.why: Paul asks, "Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?", they are baptized, and "when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them." The sequence matches Samaria closely and is the strongest parallel for treating the laying on of hands as a distinct rite following baptism.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 6:1-2 — baptisms and laying on of hands among the foundations
crossRefs.why: The writer lists "the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands" among the elementary things a congregation should already have settled. That an early Christian letter treats the imposition of hands as basic catechesis supports reading Acts 8 as describing a normal practice rather than a one-off event.

crossRefs.label: Acts 10:44-48 — the Spirit falls on Cornelius' household before baptism
crossRefs.why: At Cæsarea "the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word" while Peter was still preaching, with no laying on of hands and before any baptism. The reversed order is the main reason many interpreters read Samaria as a special moment rather than a fixed rule, and it keeps the initiative firmly with God.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the Samaritans, already validly baptized, receiving the Holy Ghost when Peter and John lay hands on them is read as the scriptural ground of confirmation as a sacrament distinct from baptism, ordinarily conferred by the bishop as one who stands in the apostles' place.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read this as an exceptional and transitional moment in which the Spirit's visible coming through the Jerusalem apostles publicly ratified the inclusion of Samaritans, so that the Church would not divide into rival Jewish and Samaritan bodies at the outset. They point to Cornelius, where the Spirit falls on Gentiles before baptism and without any imposition of hands, as evidence that Acts records varied sequences rather than a single rite. Both traditions agree that the Spirit is God's own gift and never the minister's possession, and that the episode deliberately joins the new believers to the apostolic Church rather than leaving them independent.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Peter's rebuke of Simon as the root condemnation of buying or selling sacred things and offices, a discipline the Church has legislated against ever since, and notes that the rebuke presupposes something genuinely conferred through the apostles' hands, real enough that a man would try to purchase it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree without reservation that trafficking in holy things is condemned here, but locate Simon's central error in an unconverted heart still seeking status and influence, which is why Peter addresses his heart and his need to repent rather than the price he named. Many add a warning that any account treating grace as a commodity the clergy control risks the very confusion Peter rejects. Both traditions agree that the gift of God cannot be purchased, that Peter's response is a summons to repentance and prayer rather than a bargain, and that Simon's baptism did not by itself settle the state of his heart.

verses.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
And desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem.
And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven:
And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do.
And the men which journeyed with him stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man.
And Saul arose from the earth; and when his eyes were opened, he saw no man: but they led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus.
And he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink.
And there was a certain disciple at Damascus, named Ananias; and to him said the Lord in a vision, Ananias. And he said, Behold, I am here, Lord.
And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth,
And hath seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming in, and putting his hand on him, that he might receive his sight.
Then Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem:
And here he hath authority from the chief priests to bind all that call on thy name.
But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:
For I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name’s sake.

And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost.
And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.
And when he had received meat, he was strengthened. Then was Saul certain days with the disciples which were at Damascus.
And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.

But all that heard him were amazed, and said; Is not this he that destroyed them which called on this name in Jerusalem, and came hither for that intent, that he might bring them bound unto the chief priests?
But Saul increased the more in strength, and confounded the Jews which dwelt at Damascus, proving that this is very Christ.
And after that many days were fulfilled, the Jews took counsel to kill him:
But their laying await was known of Saul. And they watched the gates day and night to kill him.
Then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket.
And when Saul was come to Jerusalem, he assayed to join himself to the disciples: but they were all afraid of him, and believed not that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared unto them how he had seen the Lord in the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how he had preached boldly at Damascus in the name of Jesus.
And he was with them coming in and going out at Jerusalem.
And he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him.
Which when the brethren knew, they brought him down to Cæsarea, and sent him forth to Tarsus.
Then had the churches rest throughout all Judæa and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied.
And it came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda.
And there he found a certain man named Æneas, which had kept his bed eight years, and was sick of the palsy.
And Peter said unto him, Æneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately.
And all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord.
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.
And it came to pass in those days, that she was sick, and died: whom when they had washed, they laid her in an upper chamber.
And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, they sent unto him two men, desiring him that he would not delay to come to them.

Then Peter arose and went with them. When he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber: and all the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them.
But Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down, and prayed; and turning him to the body said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
And he gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive.
And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord.
And it came to pass, that he tarried many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner.

chapters.summary: Saul, "yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord," secures letters for Damascus to bring "any of this way" bound to Jerusalem. Near the city "suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven"; he falls and hears, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He asks, "Who art thou, Lord?", and is answered, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest," then told to go where "it shall be told thee what thou must do." Blind three days and fasting, he prays. The Lord sends the disciple Ananias, who objects to Saul's "much evil" against the saints; the Lord replies, "he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel," and adds, "I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name’s sake." Ananias lays hands on him, calls him "Brother Saul," and "immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales"; he sees, is baptized, and "straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God." Amazement turns to plotting, and the disciples let him down "by the wall in a basket." At Jerusalem they fear him until Barnabas brings him to the apostles. With the churches at rest and "multiplied," Peter travels: at Lydda he tells palsied Æneas, "Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed," and at Joppa he prays over the dead Tabitha, says, "Tabitha, arise," and presents her alive, so that "many believed in the Lord."
takeaways: Christ identifies himself with his persecuted disciples — "why persecutest thou me?" — so that the Church is not merely a group that follows him but a body joined to him, and what is done to the least of its members is done to the Lord himself.

Grace here is sheer initiative. Saul is stopped in the middle of his errand, given no room to bargain, and named "a chosen vessel"; the vocation includes suffering from the first announcement of it, not as a later disappointment.

The convert is not left as a private visionary. The risen Lord who could have finished the work on the road instead sends him to Ananias, to sight and baptism, and afterward through Barnabas to the apostles, so an extraordinary call is verified within the ordinary community.

Peter's healing of Æneas and raising of Tabitha are done in Christ's name and out of prayer, presenting apostolic works as continuations of the Lord's own; Tabitha's "good works and almsdeeds" name the kind of life the Church grieves over and God restores.

crossRefs.label: Acts 22:6-16 — Paul retells his conversion before the crowd in Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Paul's own account adds his question, "What shall I do, Lord?", and Ananias' charge, "arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord." It fills in what Acts 9 compresses and shows that Saul understood the encounter as a commission from the start.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 1:13-24 — Paul's own account of his past and his calling
crossRefs.why: Paul admits that "beyond measure I persecuted the church of God," says he went into Arabia before Jerusalem, and reports the churches' words, "he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed." Reading it beside Acts 9 shows the same conversion told from inside, with a different interest in chronology.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:32-33 — let down by the wall in a basket at Damascus
crossRefs.why: Paul recalls that the governor under Aretas watched the city for him and that "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands." He lists it among his humiliations rather than his exploits, which colors the escape in Acts 9 as a beginning in weakness.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 1:12-16 — the persecutor who obtained mercy as a pattern
crossRefs.why: Paul calls himself "a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious" who obtained mercy, and "of whom I am chief" among sinners, saying he was shown longsuffering "for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe." It reads Acts 9 as a template of mercy rather than a singular exception.

crossRefs.label: Mark 5:35-43 — Jesus takes the dead girl by the hand and says Talitha cumi
crossRefs.why: Jesus puts the mourners out, takes the child's hand, and says, "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Peter at Joppa repeats the shape of the scene almost gesture for gesture, but kneels to pray first, marking his power as borrowed rather than his own.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the words "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" are read as revealing the Church as the body of Christ, so that the visible community of disciples is so united to him that attacking it is attacking him, which grounds the Catholic conviction that the Church is not an optional association added to faith but the form Christ's own life takes in the world.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally affirm the same union with Christ wholeheartedly, but read the identification as covenantal solidarity with all who trust him rather than as a claim about one visible institution, holding that the body is constituted by faith in Christ and includes believers wherever they are found. On this reading the verse comforts the persecuted more than it settles questions of church order. Both traditions agree that Christ counts harm done to his people as done to himself, and that no one meets him while opposing those who belong to him.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the sending of Ananias: the risen Lord, who has just appeared in person, still directs Saul into a city to wait for a disciple who lays hands on him and after which he is baptized, which is taken as a pattern of grace ordinarily reaching people through the ministry and sacraments of the Church rather than around them.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read Ananias as an instrument God freely chose, noting that the decisive encounter happened on the road with no human agent present and that God is never bound to the means he graciously uses. They often emphasize instead that Ananias' visit gave the frightened community a witness to what had really happened to their persecutor. Both traditions agree that God deliberately involved the Church in Saul's restoration, and that his calling was confirmed and received by the community rather than kept as a private matter between him and the Lord.

verses.text: There was a certain man in Cæsarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band,
A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.
He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day an angel of God coming in to him, and saying unto him, Cornelius.
And when he looked on him, he was afraid, and said, What is it, Lord? And he said unto him, Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.
And now send men to Joppa, and call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter:
He lodgeth with one Simon a tanner, whose house is by the sea side: he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do.
And when the angel which spake unto Cornelius was departed, he called two of his household servants, and a devout soldier of them that waited on him continually;
And when he had declared all these things unto them, he sent them to Joppa.
On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:
And he became very hungry, and would have eaten: but while they made ready, he fell into a trance,
And saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth:
Wherein were all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.
And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.
But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
This was done thrice: and the vessel was received up again into heaven.
Now while Peter doubted in himself what this vision which he had seen should mean, behold, the men which were sent from Cornelius had made enquiry for Simon’s house, and stood before the gate,
And called, and asked whether Simon, which was surnamed Peter, were lodged there.
While Peter thought on the vision, the Spirit said unto him, Behold, three men seek thee.
Arise therefore, and get thee down, and go with them, doubting nothing: for I have sent them.
Then Peter went down to the men which were sent unto him from Cornelius; and said, Behold, I am he whom ye seek: what is the cause wherefore ye are come?

And they said, Cornelius the centurion, a just man, and one that feareth God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews, was warned from God by an holy angel to send for thee into his house, and to hear words of thee.
Then called he them in, and lodged them. And on the morrow Peter went away with them, and certain brethren from Joppa accompanied him.
And the morrow after they entered into Cæsarea. And Cornelius waited for them, and had called together his kinsmen and near friends.
And as Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him.
But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man.
And as he talked with him, he went in, and found many that were come together.

And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
Therefore came I unto you without gainsaying, as soon as I was sent for: I ask therefore for what intent ye have sent for me?
And Cornelius said, Four days ago I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and, behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,
And said, Cornelius, thy prayer is heard, and thine alms are had in remembrance in the sight of God.
Send therefore to Joppa, and call hither Simon, whose surname is Peter; he is lodged in the house of one Simon a tanner by the sea side: who, when he cometh, shall speak unto thee.
Immediately therefore I sent to thee; and thou hast well done that thou art come. Now therefore are we all here present before God, to hear all things that are commanded thee of God.
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.
The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ: ( he is Lord of all:)
That word, I say, ye know, which was published throughout all Judæa, and began from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached;
How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
And we are witnesses of all things which he did both in the land of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they slew and hanged on a tree:
Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly;
Not to all the people, but unto witnesses chosen before of God, even to us, who did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead.
And he commanded us to preach unto the people, and to testify that it is he which was ordained of God to be the Judge of quick and dead.
To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.
While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word.
And they of the circumcision which believed were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost.
For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God. Then answered Peter,
Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?
And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Then prayed they him to tarry certain days.

chapters.summary: At Cæsarea the centurion Cornelius, "one that feared God with all his house," sees an angel who tells him, "Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God," and sends him to Joppa for Simon Peter. Next day, hungry and praying on a housetop, Peter falls into a trance and sees "a great sheet knit at the four corners" let down with "all manner of fourfooted beasts." A voice says, "Rise, Peter; kill, and eat." He refuses — "Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean" — and is answered, "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common." This is done "thrice." While he wonders what it means, the Spirit tells him three men seek him and to go "doubting nothing: for I have sent them." Peter travels to Cæsarea, lifts Cornelius from his feet — "Stand up; I myself also am a man" — and tells the household that though it is "an unlawful thing" to keep company with another nation, "God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean." He preaches that "God is no respecter of persons," and that "in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him," recounting Jesus "who went about doing good," his death, his rising, and "remission of sins" through his name. While he still speaks, "the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word." Peter asks, "Can any man forbid water," and commands them baptized.
takeaways: God prepares both parties before they meet. Cornelius' prayers and alms have already "come up for a memorial before God," and Peter's vision breaks open a boundary he would never have crossed on his own, so the apostle is converted along with the household.

"What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" is spoken about food and applied to people. Peter does not understand the vision when he receives it; its meaning arrives with the men at the gate, which is how God's word often clarifies itself in the obeying.

Peter's refusal of Cornelius' worship, "I myself also am a man," sets a limit inside apostolic authority. The office is real and God-given, yet the honor due to God is never transferable to the one who carries it.

The Spirit falls before baptism and before any question of circumcision is settled, forcing the conclusion that acceptance rests on God's own initiative rather than inherited privilege; baptism follows at once as the Church's recognition and sealing of what God has visibly begun.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 11:44-47 — the law distinguishing clean and unclean creatures
crossRefs.why: The law closes by saying its purpose is "To make a difference between the unclean and the clean," tied to the command "ye shall be holy; for I am holy." Knowing that the distinction was a matter of holiness, not hygiene, explains why Peter's "Not so, Lord" is obedience rather than stubbornness.

crossRefs.label: Mark 7:14-23 — nothing entering a man from without can defile him
crossRefs.why: Jesus teaches that defilement comes from the heart and not from food, and the evangelist adds the comment "purging all meats." Peter is being shown on the housetop what his master had already taught, which is why the vision is a reminder as much as a revelation.

crossRefs.label: Acts 11:1-18 — Peter answers for the visit before the church at Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Challenged for eating with the uncircumcised, Peter retells the whole episode and concludes, "what was I, that I could withstand God?", after which his hearers glorify God. It shows that the Cornelius event had to be received by the wider Church and was not settled by one apostle's private experience.

crossRefs.label: Acts 15:7-11 — Peter appeals to this episode at the council in Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Peter argues that God gave the Gentiles the Holy Ghost "even as he did unto us" and "put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith." Cornelius' household becomes the decisive precedent when the Church has to rule formally on the terms of Gentile membership.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 2:11-14 — Paul withstands Peter at Antioch over eating with Gentiles
crossRefs.why: Paul records that when men came from James, Peter "withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision," and that Paul rebuked him publicly. Read after Acts 10 it shows how hard the lesson was to hold, and it is often cited to stress that apostolic office does not guarantee consistent conduct.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition it is significant that the opening of the Church to the Gentiles is entrusted to Peter by direct vision rather than left to local initiative, that the Spirit tells him to go "doubting nothing," and that he is later the one whose testimony settles the matter for the whole assembly, which is read as the exercise of a distinctive Petrine role in confirming the faith of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read Peter's part as representative rather than jurisdictional: he is the fitting witness because he had been the leading apostle among the circumcision, and the narrative repeatedly stresses that God does the deciding while Peter follows instruction, asks what the vision means, and afterward has to answer to the church in Jerusalem. They also note that he needed correction over exactly this issue at Antioch. Both traditions agree that Peter genuinely stands first among the apostles in this account, and that every decisive move belongs to God rather than to any human authority.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Peter's words, that "in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him," together with the acceptance of Cornelius' prayers and alms before he ever heard the gospel, as evidence that God's grace is genuinely at work in people who have not yet been reached by preaching, while still holding that such grace is ordered toward Christ and comes to its fulfillment in the gospel and baptism.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally stress that Cornelius' devotion, however sincere, did not save him, which is precisely why an angel goes to the trouble of sending for Peter: the man must still hear the message about Jesus and believe, and only then does the Spirit fall. On this reading his God-fearing life was preparation rather than sufficiency, and the chapter is finally an argument for the necessity of preaching. Both traditions agree that God was already at work in Cornelius before Peter arrived, and that salvation is received through the name of Jesus and the remission of sins Peter announces.

verses.text: And the apostles and brethren that were in Judæa heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God.
And when Peter was come up to Jerusalem, they that were of the circumcision contended with him,
Saying, Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them.
But Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them, saying,
I was in the city of Joppa praying: and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners; and it came even to me:
Upon the which when I had fastened mine eyes, I considered, and saw fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.
And I heard a voice saying unto me, Arise, Peter; slay and eat.
But I said, Not so, Lord: for nothing common or unclean hath at any time entered into my mouth.
But the voice answered me again from heaven, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
And this was done three times: and all were drawn up again into heaven.
And, behold, immediately there were three men already come unto the house where I was, sent from Cæsarea unto me.
And the Spirit bade me go with them, nothing doubting. Moreover these six brethren accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house:
And he shewed us how he had seen an angel in his house, which stood and said unto him, Send men to Joppa, and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter;
Who shall tell thee words, whereby thou and all thy house shall be saved.
And as I began to speak, the Holy Ghost fell on them, as on us at the beginning.
Then remembered I the word of the Lord, how that he said, John indeed baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost.
Forasmuch then as God gave them the like gift as he did unto us, who believed on the Lord Jesus Christ; what was I, that I could withstand God?
When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life.
Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only.
And some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus.
And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord.
Then tidings of these things came unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem: and they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch.
Who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord.
For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith: and much people was added unto the Lord.
Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul:

And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
And in these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch.
And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Cæsar.
Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judæa:
Which also they did, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

chapters.summary: Word reaches "the apostles and brethren that were in Judæa" that "the Gentiles had also received the word of God," and when Peter comes up to Jerusalem "they that were of the circumcision contended with him," charging, "Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them." Peter answers not with argument but with narrative: he "rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order." He describes praying at Joppa and seeing "a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners" holding "fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things"; the command "Arise, Peter; slay and eat"; his refusal, "Not so, Lord"; and the answer that settles it, "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common," repeated "three times." He recounts the men sent from Cæsarea, the Spirit bidding him go "nothing doubting," and the angel who promised words "whereby thou and all thy house shall be saved." Then the decisive evidence: "as I began to speak, the Holy Ghost fell on them, as on us at the beginning," recalling the Lord's promise of baptism "with the Holy Ghost" and forcing the question, "what was I, that I could withstand God?" The objectors fall silent and glorify God. Luke turns to Antioch, where those scattered after Stephen preach to Greeks, "the hand of the Lord was with them," Barnabas is sent, fetches Saul from Tarsus, and "the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch." Agabus foretells "great dearth," and relief is sent to Judæa.
takeaways: The first great question about the Gentiles is settled by testimony rather than theory: Peter recounts what God did, and the dispute ends when the objectors recognize the same Spirit at work. Discernment in the Church begins by reading God's action before defending one's own position.

"What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" relocates the boundary between clean and unclean around God's own act rather than inherited custom, so that purity becomes a matter of hearts opened by grace.
Peter submits to being questioned by the brethren and explains himself "by order," showing that authority in the Church is exercised in the open and gives an account to the community it serves.

The name "Christians" is first given where Jew and Gentile were taught together for a whole year, and that same mixed church immediately sends material relief to Judæa. New identity and practical charity arrive together, not in sequence.

crossRefs.label: Acts 10:44-48 — the Holy Ghost falls on the Gentiles and Peter commands them to be baptized
crossRefs.why: Luke first narrates the event at Cornelius' house, where the Spirit is poured out before baptism and Peter asks, "Can any man forbid water?" Reading it alongside shows that Peter's defense in Jerusalem is an accurate report and not a later rationalization.

crossRefs.label: Acts 1:4-5 — John truly baptized with water, but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost
crossRefs.why: The risen Lord's promise before the ascension is the very word Peter says he remembered when the Spirit fell on the Gentiles. The link shows him interpreting a new event by an old promise rather than by improvisation.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 11:1-8 — the LORD distinguishes clean from unclean creatures for Israel
crossRefs.why: The law itself declares certain animals "unclean unto you," which is why Peter can honestly say nothing common had entered his mouth. Set beside the vision, it makes clear how startling the heavenly voice was and that the change came from God rather than from Peter's convenience.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 2:11-14 — Paul withstands Peter at Antioch over eating with the Gentiles
crossRefs.why: Paul reports Peter later withdrawing from Gentile tables "fearing them which were of the circumcision." Read with Acts 11, it shows how contested the practice remained even after the principle had been accepted, and that living out a conviction can lag behind confessing it.

crossRefs.label: Romans 15:25-27 — Gentile churches make a contribution for the poor saints at Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Paul describes Gentile believers who have shared in Israel's "spiritual things" repaying in "carnal things." The famine relief carried by Barnabas and Saul is the first instance of the same pattern, binding the new churches to the mother church by concrete generosity.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Peter's account here is read as the Petrine office functioning within the apostolic body: the one to whom the door of the Gentiles was first opened gives the account that settles the question for the whole church, and the brethren fall silent and glorify God once he has laid the matter out "by order."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally emphasize that Peter is summoned and questioned by the assembly rather than issuing a ruling to it, and that what persuades them is the manifest gift of the Spirit rather than his standing. They point to his own disclaimer, "what was I, that I could withstand God?", as evidence that the authority in view is God's action, not an office. Both traditions agree that the decision belongs entirely to God's initiative and that Peter's testimony was the instrument by which the Church recognized it.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads the thrice-repeated sheet and the words "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" as God himself setting aside the ceremonial separations that once marked Israel out, fulfilled now in Christ, while the moral law they served remains in force; the change is God's act received through the Church rather than a human abandonment of Scripture.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the vision as aimed chiefly at the barrier between peoples rather than at diet, since Peter applies it immediately to entering a Gentile household and eating with its members, and they are often wary of dividing the Mosaic law into tidy categories. Both traditions agree that what God has cleansed no believer may call common, and that the gospel crosses a boundary God himself has removed.

verses.text: Now about that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church.
And he killed James the brother of John with the sword.
And because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also. ( Then were the days of unleavened bread.)
And when he had apprehended him, he put him in prison, and delivered him to four quaternions of soldiers to keep him; intending after Easter to bring him forth to the people.
Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him.
And when Herod would have brought him forth, the same night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains: and the keepers before the door kept the prison.

And, behold, the angel of the Lord came upon him, and a light shined in the prison: and he smote Peter on the side, and raised him up, saying, Arise up quickly. And his chains fell off from his hands.
And the angel said unto him, Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals. And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me.
And he went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision.

When they were past the first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate that leadeth unto the city; which opened to them of his own accord: and they went out, and passed on through one street; and forthwith the angel departed from him.

And when Peter was come to himself, he said, Now I know of a surety, that the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.
And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying.
And as Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a damsel came to hearken, named Rhoda.
And when she knew Peter’s voice, she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate.
And they said unto her, Thou art mad. But she constantly affirmed that it was even so. Then said they, It is his angel.
But Peter continued knocking: and when they had opened the door, and saw him, they were astonished.

But he, beckoning unto them with the hand to hold their peace, declared unto them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, Go shew these things unto James, and to the brethren. And he departed, and went into another place.
Now as soon as it was day, there was no small stir among the soldiers, what was become of Peter.
And when Herod had sought for him, and found him not, he examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be put to death. And he went down from Judæa to Cæsarea, and there abode.

And Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon: but they came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus the king’s chamberlain their friend, desired peace; because their country was nourished by the king’s country.
And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them.
And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.
And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.
But the word of God grew and multiplied.
And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem, when they had fulfilled their ministry, and took with them John, whose surname was Mark.

chapters.summary: "Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church," kills "James the brother of John with the sword," and "because he saw it pleased the Jews" seizes Peter during "the days of unleavened bread," guarding him with "four quaternions of soldiers" and intending to bring him out afterward. The church answers with prayer, "made without ceasing of the church unto God for him." On the final night Peter sleeps "between two soldiers, bound with two chains"; an angel comes, "a light shined in the prison," and Peter is told, "Arise up quickly," and "his chains fell off from his hands." Told to gird himself and follow, Peter obeys but "wist not that it was true which was done by the angel," supposing "he saw a vision." Past the two wards, "the iron gate that leadeth unto the city" opens "of his own accord," and the angel departs. Come "to himself," Peter says, "Now I know of a surety, that the Lord hath sent his angel." At Mary's house, where "many were gathered together praying," Rhoda knows his voice and "opened not the gate for gladness"; the praying church tells her "Thou art mad," then guesses "It is his angel," until his continued knocking astonishes them. He sends word to James and departs. Herod executes the keepers, and at Cæsarea, hailed as "the voice of a god, and not of a man," is smitten "because he gave not God the glory" and "eaten of worms." "But the word of God grew and multiplied."
takeaways: Deliverance is not uniform: James dies by the sword and Peter walks free in the same chapter, so providence cannot be read off outcomes. Both men are held by the same God, and the Church's prayer is answered on terms it does not set.

The praying church struggles to believe its own prayer has been answered, which is a candid picture of faith that keeps petitioning while doubting the result. God does not withhold the deliverance because its reception is weak.
Peter sleeping soundly on the night before his trial shows a peace not drawn from circumstances, and the chains falling off become the visible sign of a freedom already interior.

Herod's end sets human acclamation against divine glory. The ruler who accepts what belongs to God alone is undone, while the word he tried to imprison "grew and multiplied" beyond any power to contain it.

crossRefs.label: Acts 5:17-25 — an angel opens the prison doors and the apostles are found teaching in the temple
crossRefs.why: An earlier arrest ends the same way, with locked doors and posted keepers proving no obstacle. The repetition establishes a pattern in Luke's narrative: human authority can imprison preachers but cannot silence the preaching.

crossRefs.label: Mark 10:35-40 — James and John are told they shall drink the cup that Jesus drinks
crossRefs.why: Jesus warns the sons of Zebedee that glory is reached through his own cup and baptism, which they confidently accept. Read beside Herod's sword, it shows James' death as the fulfillment of a promise he had already agreed to, not an accident of politics.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 34:6-7 — the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him
crossRefs.why: The psalm celebrates a poor man who cried and was saved out of all his troubles by the encamping angel. It supplies the scriptural language Peter reaches for when he says the Lord has sent his angel and delivered him.

crossRefs.label: Acts 4:23-31 — the church prays together under threat and the place is shaken
crossRefs.why: Facing official threats, the community prays not for safety but for boldness, and is filled with the Holy Ghost. It shows the practice behind the ceaseless prayer of Acts 12 and how the Church habitually responds to persecution.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 4:29-33 — Nebuchadnezzar boasts of his majesty and is driven from men
crossRefs.why: A king glories in his own power and is struck down in the very hour of his boast until he acknowledges that the most High rules. The pattern is exactly Herod's, and it frames his death as a judgment on usurped glory rather than a random calamity.

interpretationNotes.claim: The gathered believers' guess that the figure at the gate is "his angel" is taken in the Catholic tradition as reflecting an early and continuing conviction that individual believers are attended by guardian angels, a belief the Church has kept and encouraged in prayer and devotion.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally treat the remark as Luke reporting what the disciples assumed rather than a doctrine he endorses, and they caution against resting a teaching on a passing reaction from people who had just called Rhoda mad. Both traditions affirm that angels are real servants of God who act concretely for his people, which this very chapter demonstrates.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to Peter's instruction, "Go shew these things unto James, and to the brethren," followed by his departure "into another place," as a picture of James presiding over the local church at Jerusalem while Peter's ministry becomes wider than any one city, consistent with a universal Petrine role exercised alongside local bishops.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the same detail as a straightforward handover of leadership in one congregation, with James emerging as the leading elder at Jerusalem and no wider jurisdiction implied for Peter, who simply leaves to escape Herod. Both traditions agree that the earliest Church had recognized leaders, orderly communication between them, and continuity of care when an individual was removed.

verses.text: Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
So they, being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, departed unto Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus.
And when they were at Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews: and they had also John to their minister.
And when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar-jesus:
Which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer ( for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith.
Then Saul, ( who also is called Paul,) filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him,
And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand.
Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord.
Now when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia: and John departing from them returned to Jerusalem.
But when they departed from Perga, they came to Antioch in Pisidia, and went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and sat down.
And after the reading of the law and the prophets the rulers of the synagogue sent unto them, saying, Ye men and brethren, if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on.
Then Paul stood up, and beckoning with his hand said, Men of Israel, and ye that fear God, give audience.
The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, and with an high arm brought he them out of it.
And about the time of forty years suffered he their manners in the wilderness.
And when he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Chanaan, he divided their land to them by lot.
And after that he gave unto them judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years, until Samuel the prophet.
And afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years.

And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.
Of this man’s seed hath God according to his promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus:
When John had first preached before his coming the baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
And as John fulfilled his course, he said, Whom think ye that I am? I am not he. But, behold, there cometh one after me, whose shoes of his feet I am not worthy to loose.
Men and brethren, children of the stock of Abraham, and whosoever among you feareth God, to you is the word of this salvation sent.
For they that dwell at Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they knew him not, nor yet the voices of the prophets which are read every sabbath day, they have fulfilled them in condemning him.
And though they found no cause of death in him, yet desired they Pilate that he should be slain.
And when they had fulfilled all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a sepulchre.
But God raised him from the dead:
And he was seen many days of them which came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses unto the people.
And we declare unto you glad tidings, how that the promise which was made unto the fathers,
God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.
And as concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he said on this wise, I will give you the sure mercies of David.
Wherefore he saith also in another psalm, Thou shalt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
For David, after he had served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers, and saw corruption:
But he, whom God raised again, saw no corruption.
Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins:
And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.
Beware therefore, lest that come upon you, which is spoken of in the prophets;
Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.
And when the Jews were gone out of the synagogue, the Gentiles besought that these words might be preached to them the next sabbath.
Now when the congregation was broken up, many of the Jews and religious proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas: who, speaking to them, persuaded them to continue in the grace of God.
And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God.
But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.

Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.
For so hath the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.
And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.
And the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts.
But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came unto Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost.

chapters.summary: At Antioch, among "certain prophets and teachers" including Barnabas, Manaen and Saul, "as they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." Having "fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them," the church sends them away "being sent forth by the Holy Ghost." In Cyprus the sorcerer Bar-jesus "withstood them"; Saul, "who also is called Paul," filled with the Holy Ghost, names him "thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness" and strikes him blind "for a season," and the deputy believes, "being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord." John leaves them at Perga. In the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia Paul traces Israel's story from Egypt through the judges to David, "a man after mine own heart," and to "this man’s seed," from which God "raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus." Jerusalem's rulers, not knowing "the voices of the prophets which are read every sabbath day," fulfilled them in condemning him, "But God raised him from the dead." Paul applies the psalms, "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee" and "Thou shalt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption," announcing that in Christ "all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses." Almost the whole city gathers the next sabbath; envy follows, the apostles turn "to the Gentiles," and though expelled the disciples remain "filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost."
takeaways: The mission begins inside worship: the Spirit speaks while the church is ministering and fasting. Mission is therefore not a program the Church invents but a call it hears, tests, and confirms.

Barnabas and Saul are already called by the Spirit and still receive fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands. Divine call and churchly commissioning are not rivals; the visible act ratifies a vocation it does not manufacture.

Paul preaches the gospel as the continuation of Israel's history rather than a break from it. The God who chose the fathers, bore with them in the wilderness, and raised up David has kept the same promise by raising Jesus.

Justification is announced as something the law of Moses could not accomplish and that reaches "all that believe," while the hearers remain free to "judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life." Grace offered is never grace coerced.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 27:18-23 — Moses lays his hands on Joshua and gives him a charge before the congregation
crossRefs.why: God commands that a man "in whom is the spirit" be commissioned publicly by the imposition of hands, with honour put upon him before all the people. It is the Old Testament root of the gesture at Antioch and shows the rite conveying office, not merely good wishes.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 4:14 — the gift given by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery
crossRefs.why: Paul later describes a gift residing in Timothy that came through prophecy and the hands of the elders. Read with Acts 13, it shows the same combination of prophetic word and imposed hands becoming the settled practice of the churches Paul founded.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 2:7 — Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee
crossRefs.why: Paul cites this decree as fulfilled in the resurrection rather than merely in Jesus' birth. Reading the psalm whole shows the enthronement of God's anointed against raging nations, which is precisely the claim Paul is making in a hostile synagogue.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 49:6 — I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles
crossRefs.why: The servant's commission extends beyond restoring Israel to becoming God's salvation "unto the end of the earth." Paul quotes it as a command laid on him and Barnabas, so the turn to the Gentiles is presented as obedience to prophecy rather than reaction to rejection.

crossRefs.label: Romans 3:20-28 — the righteousness of God apart from the law, for all that believe
crossRefs.why: Paul's letter unfolds at length what the sermon states briefly, that no flesh is justified by the deeds of the law and that righteousness comes through faith in Christ. It is the fullest commentary Paul himself gives on his own synagogue preaching.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the fasting, prayer and laying on of hands before Barnabas and Saul are sent out is read as an early instance of ordination: a grace and an office conferred through a visible rite performed by the leaders of the church, which is why the Church continues to ordain by prayer and the imposition of hands rather than by acclamation or self-appointment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the gesture as a solemn commissioning and blessing for a particular missionary task rather than the conferral of a permanent sacramental character, noting that Barnabas and Saul were already reckoned among the prophets and teachers and that the church is releasing them for a journey they later come back to report on. Both traditions agree that ministry is given and confirmed by the Church acting under the Spirit, and is never self-assumed.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses" as teaching that justification comes wholly through Christ and never through works of the Mosaic law, while holding that the grace so given really transforms the believer, which is why Paul and Barnabas then urge their hearers "to continue in the grace of God."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the verse as a compact statement of justification by faith alone, reading "all that believe" as making faith the sole instrument by which Christ's righteousness is received, with obedience following as fruit rather than forming any part of the ground. Both traditions confess that no one is justified by law-keeping and that justification is the free gift of God in Christ.

verses.text: And it came to pass in Iconium, that they went both together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spake, that a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed.
But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles, and made their minds evil affected against the brethren.
Long time therefore abode they speaking boldly in the Lord, which gave testimony unto the word of his grace, and granted signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
But the multitude of the city was divided: and part held with the Jews, and part with the apostles.
And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them,
They were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about:
And there they preached the gospel.
And there sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, being a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked:
The same heard Paul speak: who stedfastly beholding him, and perceiving that he had faith to be healed,
Said with a loud voice, Stand upright on thy feet. And he leaped and walked.
And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.
And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker.
Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people.
Which when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of, they rent their clothes, and ran in among the people, crying out,

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
Who in times past suffered all nations to walk in their own ways.
Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
And with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them.
And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.
Howbeit, as the disciples stood round about him, he rose up, and came into the city: and the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe.
And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch,
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
And after they had passed throughout Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.
And when they had preached the word in Perga, they went down into Attalia:
And thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled.
And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles.
And there they abode long time with the disciples.

chapters.summary: At Iconium they speak in the synagogue "that a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed," while unbelievers make the Gentiles' minds "evil affected against the brethren." They stay "long time" nonetheless, "speaking boldly in the Lord," who "granted signs and wonders to be done by their hands," until the city divides and an assault is prepared "to use them despitefully, and to stone them." Fleeing to Lystra and Derbe, they preach; Paul sees a cripple "from his mother’s womb," perceives "that he had faith to be healed," and says, "Stand upright on thy feet," and "he leaped and walked." The crowd cries "in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men," and the priest of Jupiter brings "oxen and garlands." The apostles "rent their clothes," run in and protest, "We also are men of like passions with you," urging them to "turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea," who "left not himself without witness" in "rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons." Barely restrained, the same crowd is soon turned by Jews from Antioch and Iconium, and Paul is stoned and dragged out "supposing he had been dead," yet rises and goes on. Returning through those cities they confirm the disciples, teaching that "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God," ordain "elders in every church," pray with fasting, and report at Antioch how God "had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles."
takeaways: The crowd that would sacrifice to Paul stones him soon after. Adulation and violence lie closer together than they appear, and the apostles refuse both by insisting they are "men of like passions with you."

Paul's appeal to rain, fruitful seasons, and hearts filled "with food and gladness" grants that God has always given the nations a real witness of himself, so the gospel arrives naming a Giver they have long been receiving from.

The apostles do not promise exemption from suffering; they interpret it. Tribulation is the road into the kingdom rather than evidence of having wandered off it, which is why the same word that converts also confirms.

Evangelization does not end at conversion. They walk back through hostile cities to strengthen believers and appoint elders, so that new churches receive both continuing care and a settled ordering before the founders leave.

crossRefs.label: Acts 3:1-10 — Peter heals a man lame from his mother's womb, who goes walking and leaping
crossRefs.why: Luke tells an almost identical healing through Peter, down to the lifelong lameness and the leaping. The deliberate parallel presents Paul's ministry among the Gentiles as continuous in power and pattern with Peter's among the Jews.

crossRefs.label: Acts 17:22-31 — Paul at Athens preaches the God who made the world and gives all things
crossRefs.why: Facing another pagan audience, Paul again starts from the Creator who gives "life, and breath, and all things" rather than from Israel's scriptures. Read together, the two speeches show a consistent method for addressing those with no biblical background.

crossRefs.label: Romans 1:19-23 — what may be known of God is manifest, yet the glory of God is exchanged for images
crossRefs.why: Paul argues that God's power is "clearly seen" in what he has made, and that idolatry is a turning of that knowledge into images. Lystra dramatizes the letter's claim, as a genuine act of God is immediately misread into a pagan story.

crossRefs.label: 2 Timothy 3:10-12 — persecutions which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra
crossRefs.why: Paul names these exact cities when reminding Timothy what he endured and that the Lord delivered him out of all of it. It confirms Luke's account from Paul's own memory and generalizes it: all who will live godly shall suffer persecution.

crossRefs.label: Titus 1:5 — ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee
crossRefs.why: Paul instructs a delegate to complete what is lacking by appointing elders city by city. The near-identical phrasing shows the practice of Acts 14 hardening into a standing instruction for how new churches are to be finished and governed.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the apostles ordaining "elders in every church," with prayer and fasting, is read as evidence that the apostolic mission deliberately provided a permanent ordered ministry able to continue after the founders departed, which grounds the Catholic understanding of apostolic succession and the ordination of presbyters for each local community.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that the apostles installed local leaders, but read the appointment as recognizing qualified men to teach and govern particular congregations rather than as transmitting a priestly order, and many stress that the elders are commended "to the Lord, on whom they believed" rather than to a chain of office. Both traditions agree that Christ's churches are not left leaderless and that such leadership is conferred through the Church rather than seized.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Paul's argument that God "left not himself without witness" in rain and fruitful seasons as support for the conviction that something true about God can be known by reason from the world he has made, so that grace comes to a nature already capable of receiving it rather than to a blank.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally acknowledge the same witness in creation but emphasize how little it accomplishes on its own, since it leaves people without excuse rather than leading them to God, and Lystra proves the point when a real miracle produces immediate idolatry. Both traditions affirm that creation truly testifies to its Maker and that the gospel must still be preached for anyone to know him rightly.
