verses.text: And certain men which came down from Judæa taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
And being brought on their way by the church, they passed through Phenice and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles: and they caused great joy unto all the brethren.
And when they were come to Jerusalem, they were received of the church, and of the apostles and elders, and they declared all things that God had done with them.
But there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.

And when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up, and said unto them, Men and brethren, ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe.
And God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us;
And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.
Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.
Then all the multitude kept silence, and gave audience to Barnabas and Paul, declaring what miracles and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them.
And after they had held their peace, James answered, saying, Men and brethren, hearken unto me:
Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.
And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written,
After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down; and I will build again the ruins thereof, and I will set it up:
That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called, saith the Lord, who doeth all these things.
Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.
Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God:
But that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood.
For Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath day.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
And they wrote letters by them after this manner; The apostles and elders and brethren send greeting unto the brethren which are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia:

Forasmuch as we have heard, that certain which went out from us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law: to whom we gave no such commandment:
It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men unto you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who shall also tell you the same things by mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well.
So when they were dismissed, they came to Antioch: and when they had gathered the multitude together, they delivered the epistle:
Which when they had read, they rejoiced for the consolation.
And Judas and Silas, being prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed them.
And after they had tarried there a space, they were let go in peace from the brethren unto the apostles.
Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still.
Paul also and Barnabas continued in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.
And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark.
But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work.
And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus;
And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God.
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.

chapters.summary: Men from Judæa teach at Antioch, "Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved," and Paul and Barnabas have "no small dissension and disputation," so they are sent "up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question." Travelling through Samaria "declaring the conversion of the Gentiles," they cause "great joy," but believing Pharisees insist "that it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses." The apostles and elders gather "to consider of this matter," and after "much disputing" Peter rises: God chose that "the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel," gave them the Spirit, "put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith," and warns against "a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear," since "through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." Barnabas and Paul recount the miracles. James answers, joins "the words of the prophets" about "the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down," and gives his "sentence" that the Gentiles not be troubled, but written to about "pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood." The church sends Judas and Silas with a letter: "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden." Antioch "rejoiced for the consolation." Later Paul and Barnabas part over Mark in a contention "so sharp," and each mission goes on.
takeaways: The gospel's first doctrinal crisis is settled neither by private revelation nor by the strongest personality, but by the Church deliberating together, weighing testimony and Scripture, and issuing a judgment it dares to attribute to the Holy Ghost as well as to itself.

Peter's "purifying their hearts by faith" and "we shall be saved, even as they" put Jew and Gentile on identical ground. Grace, not ancestry or observance, is what saves, and any added requirement functions as a yoke rather than a help.

The abstentions imposed are pastoral rather than a reinstatement of the law. They guard conscience and shared tables in mixed communities where "Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him," so that liberty is exercised without wounding neighbors.

The chapter ends with an unresolved quarrel between two good men, and Luke does not tidy it away. The same Church capable of a Spirit-guided common decision still contains sharp personal conflict, and the mission advances through both.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 2:1-10 — Paul lays his gospel before the pillars at Jerusalem and Titus is not compelled
crossRefs.why: Paul gives his own account of going up to Jerusalem, refusing circumcision for Titus, and receiving "the right hands of fellowship" from James, Cephas and John. It supplies the participant's perspective on the same struggle Luke narrates from outside.

crossRefs.label: Acts 11:1-18 — Peter explains the Gentile conversion and the circumcision party is silenced
crossRefs.why: The earlier hearing establishes the precedent Peter now invokes, that God gave the Gentiles the Spirit before any observance was required of them. Reading it first shows the council is not deciding a novelty but confirming what had already been recognized.

crossRefs.label: Amos 9:11-12 — I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, that the heathen may be called by my name
crossRefs.why: The prophet promises a restored house of David that gathers the nations called by God's name. James cites it to show that the ingathering of Gentiles is what the prophets foretold, making the decision an act of obedience to Scripture rather than an accommodation to circumstance.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 5:1-6 — stand fast in liberty and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage
crossRefs.why: Paul warns that accepting circumcision as necessary makes a man "a debtor to do the whole law" and empties Christ of profit for him. It is the theological argument behind Peter's image of an unbearable yoke, pressed to its conclusion.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:15-20 — tell it unto the church, and where two or three are gathered in my name
crossRefs.why: Jesus makes the assembled community the final court in a disputed matter, promises that its binding and loosing hold in heaven, and pledges his presence where it gathers in his name. It is the charter behind a council that can write "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us."

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the gathering at Jerusalem is read as the pattern for how the Church settles disputed questions of faith: the apostles and elders come together to consider the matter, testimony and Scripture are weighed in open debate, a sentence is formulated, and the result is written out and sent as binding on churches that were never present. The phrase "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us" is taken as evidence that Christ's promised guidance really operates through the deliberate judgment of the Church's assembled pastors, and not only through each believer's private reading.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally honor the assembly as a genuine and exemplary model of corporate discernment while denying that it establishes a standing office of infallible teaching. On their reading its decision carries weight precisely because it is shown to rest on God's manifest act and on the prophets, "to this agree the words of the prophets," so that its authority is derived from Scripture rather than independent of it, and every later gathering must be tested the same way. Both traditions affirm that the Church is meant to decide such questions together rather than in isolation, and that the Holy Ghost was truly at work in what was determined at Jerusalem.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the order of the speeches: Peter rises first, ends "much disputing," and states the principle that God "put no difference between us and them," after which James applies it pastorally and gives his "sentence." This is understood as a Petrine primacy exercised inside the apostolic college rather than over it, with the local head of the Jerusalem church working out what Peter has settled.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally note that it is James who pronounces the decisive "my sentence," and that the letter goes out in the name of "the apostles and elders and brethren" with "the whole church" concurring, which suggests a collegial decision with no single ruling voice. On this reading Peter contributes weighty testimony rather than a verdict. Both traditions agree that Peter's witness was pivotal to the outcome and that the assembly reached its conclusion "with one accord."

verses.text: Then came he to Derbe and Lystra: and, behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus, the son of a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed; but his father was a Greek:
Which was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium.
Him would Paul have to go forth with him; and took and circumcised him because of the Jews which were in those quarters: for they knew all that his father was a Greek.
And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem.
And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily.
Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,
After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not.
And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.
Therefore loosing from Troas, we came with a straight course to Samothracia, and the next day to Neapolis;
And from thence to Philippi, which is the chief city of that part of Macedonia, and a colony: and we were in that city abiding certain days.
And on the sabbath we went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made; and we sat down, and spake unto the women which resorted thither.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us.
And it came to pass, as we went to prayer, a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met us, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying:
The same followed Paul and us, and cried, saying, These men are the servants of the most high God, which shew unto us the way of salvation.
And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour.
And when her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone, they caught Paul and Silas, and drew them into the marketplace unto the rulers,
And brought them to the magistrates, saying, These men, being Jews, do exceedingly trouble our city,
And teach customs, which are not lawful for us to receive, neither to observe, being Romans.
And the multitude rose up together against them: and the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them.
And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely:
Who, having received such a charge, thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.
And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.
Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas,
And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?
And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.
And they spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house.
And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway.
And when he had brought them into his house, he set meat before them, and rejoiced, believing in God with all his house.
And when it was day, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go.
And the keeper of the prison told this saying to Paul, The magistrates have sent to let you go: now therefore depart, and go in peace.

But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans.
And they came and besought them, and brought them out, and desired them to depart out of the city.
And they went out of the prison, and entered into the house of Lydia: and when they had seen the brethren, they comforted them, and departed.

chapters.summary: Paul returns to Derbe and Lystra, takes Timothy, "well reported of by the brethren," circumcises him for the Jews there, and delivers the decrees "ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem," so the churches are "established in the faith." They are "forbidden of the Holy Ghost" to preach in Asia and turned back from Bithynia because "the Spirit suffered them not," until at Troas a vision pleads, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us," swinging the mission west as the narrative shifts to "we." At Philippi, at a riverside place of prayer, Lydia "a seller of purple" listens, "whose heart the Lord opened," and "when she was baptized, and her household," she constrains them to lodge with her. A slave girl with "a spirit of divination" trails them crying that they "shew unto us the way of salvation," until Paul, "being grieved," commands the spirit out. Her owners, seeing "the hope of their gains was gone," drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates; they are beaten, jailed, and put in stocks. At midnight they "prayed, and sang praises unto God"; an earthquake opens every door; the jailer draws his sword and hears, "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here." He asks, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" and hears, "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house." Baptized "he and all his, straightway," he feeds them, rejoicing "believing in God with all his house." Paul then refuses a quiet release, claiming Roman citizenship.
takeaways: The mission advances by the Spirit's closed doors as much as by its open ones: Paul is "forbidden" Asia and blocked from Bithynia before the Macedonian call comes, so guidance is often recognized only in retrospect.
Lydia's conversion is described first as God's act, "whose heart the Lord opened," yet her attention, faith, and insistent hospitality are genuinely hers, holding grace and free response together.
Salvation is announced to a household, not merely to an individual: the promise runs "and thy house," and baptism follows for the whole family and its dependents together.

Praise in the dark precedes the earthquake. The freedom the gospel gives is interior first, which is why the prisoners stay when the doors open and the jailer ends the night a believer rather than a suicide.

crossRefs.label: Acts 15:22-29 — the decrees of the apostles and elders sent to the Gentile churches
crossRefs.why: The council's letter, sent because "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us," settles what Gentile believers must observe. Acts 16 shows Paul carrying those very decrees from city to city, which is why circumcising Timothy for the sake of the Jews contradicts nothing that was decided.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 1:3-6 — thanksgiving for the Philippians' fellowship in the gospel from the first day
crossRefs.why: Years later Paul writes to the church founded in this chapter, recalling "your fellowship in the gospel from the first day until now" and trusting that God "will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." Reading it alongside shows what grew from a riverside prayer meeting and a jailer's household.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:13-17 — Paul recalls baptizing the household of Stephanas
crossRefs.why: Listing the few he personally baptized, Paul names "the household of Stephanas," another whole house received at once. Read with Lydia and the jailer, it presents household baptism as a settled apostolic practice rather than an isolated incident.

crossRefs.label: Romans 10:9-13 — confess with thy mouth and believe in thine heart, and thou shalt be saved
crossRefs.why: Paul states in doctrinal form what he told the jailer, that believing in the risen Lord and confessing him brings salvation to everyone who calls on his name. Protestant interpreters generally read the two texts together as making personal faith the thing that baptism presupposes and expresses.

crossRefs.label: Acts 12:5-11 — Peter delivered from prison while the church prays without ceasing
crossRefs.why: An angel wakes Peter and "his chains fell off from his hands" while the church prays through the night. The deliberate parallel with Paul and Silas at midnight presents God's opening of prisons as a recurring sign that the word cannot be bound.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the baptism of Lydia "and her household" and of the jailer "he and all his" is read as evidence that the apostles baptized entire houses, children and dependents included, on the faith of the head of the family, and this apostolic pattern is one of the scriptural grounds for infant baptism.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters are divided rather than uniform here: many Reformed, Lutheran, and Anglican readers baptize infants for much the same covenantal reasons, while Baptist and free-church interpreters note that Paul and Silas "spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house," and that the jailer "rejoiced, believing in God with all his house," suggesting that everyone baptized had first heard and believed. Both traditions affirm that baptism truly joins a person to Christ, and that the initiative belongs to God rather than to the one being baptized.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul" as a portrait of grace going before: God moves first and interiorly, yet Lydia's listening, believing, and constraining hospitality are her own free acts, so grace enables the will rather than bypassing it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that the opening of the heart is wholly God's work, and those in the Reformed stream press it further, reading it as an effectual grace that certainly produces faith rather than merely making faith possible. Both traditions confess that no one believes unless God first acts upon the heart, and that the faith which follows is a real human response for which the believer is not a passive object.

verses.text: Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where was a synagogue of the Jews:
And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures,
Opening and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ.
And some of them believed, and consorted with Paul and Silas; and of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women not a few.

But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people.
And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also;
Whom Jason hath received: and these all do contrary to the decrees of Cæsar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus.
And they troubled the people and the rulers of the city, when they heard these things.
And when they had taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go.
And the brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night unto Berea: who coming thither went into the synagogue of the Jews.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Therefore many of them believed; also of honourable women which were Greeks, and of men, not a few.
But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was preached of Paul at Berea, they came thither also, and stirred up the people.
And then immediately the brethren sent away Paul to go as it were to the sea: but Silas and Timotheus abode there still.
And they that conducted Paul brought him unto Athens: and receiving a commandment unto Silas and Timotheus for to come to him with all speed, they departed.
Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry.
Therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met with him.

Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
And they took him, and brought him unto Areopagus, saying, May we know what this new doctrine, whereof thou speakest, is?
For thou bringest certain strange things to our ears: we would know therefore what these things mean.
( For all the Athenians and strangers which were there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell, or to hear some new thing.)
Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars’ hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
Neither is worshipped with men’s hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man’s device.
And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:

Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead.
And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
So Paul departed from among them.
Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

chapters.summary: At Thessalonica Paul, "as his manner was," reasons three sabbaths from the scriptures, arguing "that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead." Some believe, but a mob assails Jason, charging that these men "have turned the world upside down" and proclaim "another king, one Jesus." Sent by night to Berea, Paul finds hearers "more noble," who "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so," until agitators arrive from Thessalonica. At Athens his "spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry," and he disputes daily until philosophers who call him a "babbler" and "a setter forth of strange gods" bring him to the Areopagus. He begins from an altar inscribed "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD," declaring the Creator who "dwelleth not in temples made with hands," needs nothing, "giveth to all life, and breath, and all things," and "hath made of one blood all nations of men," fixing their times and boundaries so that "they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him." Quoting their own poets, "in him we live, and move, and have our being," he argues that God's offspring should not imagine the Godhead as shaped metal or stone. Past ignorance God "winked at"; now he "commandeth all men every where to repent," having appointed a day of judgment and given assurance by raising the ordained man. At the resurrection "some mocked," others deferred, a few believed, among them Dionysius and Damaris.
takeaways: God can be genuinely known from what he has made. Paul argues from creation, providence, and the human search before he ever names Christ, treating pagan longing as a real if distorted reaching after the true God.

Natural knowledge does not suffice on its own: the speech moves from an altar to an unknown god toward repentance and a coming judgment, because only the risen Christ turns religious ignorance into accountable faith.
The Bereans model an examined faith, receiving the preached word eagerly and testing it against the Scriptures, so docility and scrutiny belong together rather than standing opposed.

The gospel's public reception is mixed by nature, mockery and postponement and belief arriving in the same hour, and Paul measures the day by faithful preaching rather than by the size of the response.

crossRefs.label: Romans 1:18-25 — the invisible things of God clearly seen by the things that are made
crossRefs.why: Paul writes that "the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made," leaving idolaters "without excuse" once they exchange the Creator for the creature. It is the doctrinal form of the Areopagus argument, and the Catholic tradition draws on both when it holds that God can be known with certainty by the light of natural reason.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 19:1-6 — the heavens declare the glory of God
crossRefs.why: The psalm says "The heavens declare the glory of God" in a testimony given without words, since "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." It supplies the Old Testament root of Paul's claim that the Creator has never been silent, even toward nations that never received the law.

crossRefs.label: Acts 14:14-17 — God left not himself without witness among the nations
crossRefs.why: At Lystra Paul tells another pagan crowd to "turn from these vanities unto the living God," who "left not himself without witness" in rain and fruitful seasons. The earlier speech shows that the Areopagus address is Paul's settled approach to Gentiles rather than a single experiment in Athens.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 2:1-5 — Paul determined to know nothing save Jesus Christ, and him crucified
crossRefs.why: Writing to Corinth, the city he goes to next, Paul says he came "not with excellency of speech or of wisdom" and "determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." Protestant interpreters often read this as Paul's own commentary on Athens, a caution that philosophical common ground must yield quickly to the preached cross.

crossRefs.label: 1 Thessalonians 1:5-10 — they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God
crossRefs.why: Paul's letter to the church founded at the start of this chapter describes converts who "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" and now wait for his Son from heaven. It shows the Thessalonian mission bearing durable fruit despite the riot that cut the visit short.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition treats the Areopagus speech as a scriptural warrant for natural theology: because "God that made the world and all things therein" is "not far from every one of us," human reason can reach a real if incomplete knowledge of the Creator prior to revelation, so philosophy and honest pagan longing can genuinely prepare a person to receive the gospel.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally affirm that creation testifies to God, but many stress that this testimony chiefly removes excuses rather than building a natural knowledge that leads anyone to him, since fallen minds reliably convert what they perceive into idols, which is precisely what Paul finds in Athens. They also note that Paul cites the poets to indict the city rather than to endorse its wisdom, and that the speech turns on repentance and the resurrection. Both traditions hold that God has truly made himself known through what he has made, and that no one is saved apart from hearing and believing the gospel of the risen Christ.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the Bereans are praised for testing the apostolic preaching against the Scriptures only after they had "received the word with all readiness of mind," which is read as showing the written word and the living apostolic proclamation working together: the Scriptures confirm the preaching, and the preaching supplies the interpretation under which the texts are searched.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the same verse as an early warrant for the Scriptures standing as the final norm, since even an apostle's message is checked against them and the hearers are called "more noble" for doing so. Both traditions agree that Scripture is the God-given standard, that hearers should examine what they are taught rather than accept it passively, and that searching with readiness of mind is a different disposition from suspicion.

verses.text: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth;
And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them.
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks.
And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ.
And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.
And he departed thence, and entered into a certain man’s house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue.
And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house; and many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized.
Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace:
For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city.
And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
Saying, This fellow persuadeth men to worship God contrary to the law.
And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, reason would that I should bear with you:
But if it be a question of words and names, and of your law, look ye to it; for I will be no judge of such matters.
And he drave them from the judgment seat.
Then all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things.

And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow.
And he came to Ephesus, and left them there: but he himself entered into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews.
When they desired him to tarry longer time with them, he consented not;
But bade them farewell, saying, I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem: but I will return again unto you, if God will. And he sailed from Ephesus.
And when he had landed at Cæsarea, and gone up, and saluted the church, he went down to Antioch.
And after he had spent some time there, he departed, and went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.
And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus.
This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.
And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace:
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.

chapters.summary: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth and lodges with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews expelled from Rome, working beside them because "by their occupation they were tentmakers." He reasons in the synagogue every sabbath, and when Silas and Timothy arrive he is "pressed in the spirit," testifying "that Jesus was Christ." Opposed and blasphemed, he shakes his raiment: "Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles." He moves next door to the house of Justus; Crispus, "the chief ruler of the synagogue," believes "with all his house," and many Corinthians "believed, and were baptized." A night vision steadies him, "Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace," with the promise "I have much people in this city," and he stays "a year and six months, teaching the word of God." Hauled before Gallio, he hears the deputy dismiss the charge as "a question of words and names, and of your law" and drive the accusers off, unmoved when Sosthenes is beaten there. Paul later sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, "having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow," reasons briefly at Ephesus, promises to return "if God will," and travels on "strengthening all the disciples." Meanwhile Apollos, "an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures," teaches at Ephesus while "knowing only the baptism of John"; Aquila and Priscilla take him aside and "expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly," after which he crosses to Achaia and "mightily convinced the Jews" that Jesus was Christ.
takeaways: Paul supports himself at the workbench with Aquila and Priscilla, so apostolic ministry is shown carrying its own weight rather than trading on the gospel; ordinary labor and preaching stand side by side.
The promise "I have much people in this city" is spoken before those people believe, so mission proceeds on God's prior knowledge and call rather than on visible results.
A married lay couple corrects and completes the teaching of a gifted preacher, showing that handing on the faith belongs to the whole believing community and that even the learned need catechizing.

Gallio's refusal to adjudicate "a question of words and names" buys the young church legal breathing room, and God's providence works as readily through an indifferent magistrate as through an earthquake.

crossRefs.label: Romans 16:3-5 — greet Priscilla and Aquila, and the church that is in their house
crossRefs.why: Paul later greets the same couple as "my helpers in Christ Jesus" and salutes "the church that is in their house." The link shows the tentmakers of Corinth becoming long-term partners in the mission and hosts of a congregation in their own home.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 3:4-11 — I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase
crossRefs.why: The Corinthian factions that say "I am of Paul" against "I am of Apollos" arise from the two ministries this chapter introduces. Paul's answer, "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase," reads Acts 18 as one work carried out by different hands under a single Lord.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 33:1-9 — the watchman who must warn or answer for the blood of the people
crossRefs.why: God sets Ezekiel as "a watchman unto the house of Israel," whose failure to sound the trumpet makes him answerable for those who perish. Paul's "I am clean" before the Corinthian synagogue is spoken in exactly this idiom, claiming a duty discharged rather than an indifference to the lost.

crossRefs.label: Acts 19:1-7 — the Ephesian disciples who knew only the baptism of John
crossRefs.why: The next chapter finds about a dozen men at Ephesus in the same partial condition as Apollos, baptized only into the baptism of John, and completes their initiation. Read together, the two episodes show the Church actively bringing sincere but unfinished faith into its full apostolic form.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 6:1-5 — the Nazarite vow and the unshorn head
crossRefs.why: The law describes a voluntary vow of separation to the LORD during which "there shall no razor come upon his head" until the days are fulfilled. It supplies the background for Paul shearing his head at Cenchrea and shows a freely undertaken devotional vow kept by the apostle who preaches grace.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition points to Apollos, a man "mighty in the scriptures" who "taught diligently the things of the Lord" and still needed to be taught "the way of God more perfectly," as showing that Scripture, however ably studied, is handed on and completed within the apostolic community, so the living transmission of the faith is not a rival to the written word but its ordinary setting.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally observe that what Apollos lacked was not a tradition standing beside Scripture but the completed apostolic gospel itself, especially the events following the baptism of John, and they note that a lay couple rather than an office-holder supplies it. Both traditions agree that no one reads the Scriptures well in isolation, and that sincere and eloquent teaching can be genuinely incomplete until the wider Church corrects it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Paul's vow at Cenchrea and his resolve to "keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem" as evidence that freely chosen devotional commitments, seasons, and bodily observances remain fitting under grace, and finds here a scriptural root for the Church's practice of vows and its liturgical calendar.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the vow as Paul's personal liberty and his accommodation to Jewish sensibilities for the sake of the mission, not a pattern binding on Christians, and they warn against turning voluntary devotion into obligation. Both traditions agree that vows and observances have no power to justify, that Paul is not reimposing the law he argued against elsewhere, and that such practices are worth keeping only insofar as they serve living faith in Christ.

verses.text: And it came to pass, that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul having passed through the upper coasts came to Ephesus: and finding certain disciples,
He said unto them, Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed? And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost.
And he said unto them, Unto what then were ye baptized? And they said, Unto John’s baptism.
Then said Paul, John verily baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying unto the people, that they should believe on him which should come after him, that is, on Christ Jesus.
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them; and they spake with tongues, and prophesied.
And all the men were about twelve.
And he went into the synagogue, and spake boldly for the space of three months, disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God.
But when divers were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil of that way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus.
And this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
And God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul:
So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.
Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.
And there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew, and chief of the priests, which did so.
And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
And this was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus; and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
And many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds.
Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed.
After these things were ended, Paul purposed in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, After I have been there, I must also see Rome.
So he sent into Macedonia two of them that ministered unto him, Timotheus and Erastus; but he himself stayed in Asia for a season.
And the same time there arose no small stir about that way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;
Whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth.
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.
And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.
And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.
And when Paul would have entered in unto the people, the disciples suffered him not.
And certain of the chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre.
Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.
And they drew Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. And Alexander beckoned with the hand, and would have made his defence unto the people.
But when they knew that he was a Jew, all with one voice about the space of two hours cried out, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.

And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
Seeing then that these things cannot be spoken against, ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly.
For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess.
Wherefore if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another.
But if ye enquire any thing concerning other matters, it shall be determined in a lawful assembly.
For we are in danger to be called in question for this day’s uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse.
And when he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.

chapters.summary: At Ephesus Paul meets "certain disciples" and asks, "Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?" They answer, "We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost," knowing only the baptism of John, which Paul explains pointed forward to Christ; they are "baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus," and when he "had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them," and they speak with tongues and prophesy, "about twelve" in all. He preaches boldly in the synagogue three months, then withdraws to "the school of one Tyrannus" two years, "so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus." God works "special miracles by the hands of Paul," healing through "handkerchiefs or aprons" from his body. When the seven sons of Sceva try the formula "We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth," the evil spirit answers, "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?" and the man drives them out "naked and wounded." Fear falls on the city, believers confess their deeds, and those who used "curious arts" burn books worth "fifty thousand pieces of silver": "So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed." Paul plans for Jerusalem: "I must also see Rome." Then Demetrius, whose trade in "silver shrines for Diana" is threatened, rallies the craftsmen, "by this craft we have our wealth," and the city chants "Great is Diana of the Ephesians" for two hours in the theatre until the townclerk quiets them and dismisses the assembly.
takeaways: Christian initiation in Acts is not one undifferentiated moment: these disciples are baptized into Christ and then receive the Spirit through the apostle's laying on of hands, tying the gift of the Spirit to an act of the Church rather than to private experience.

The name of Jesus is not a technique. The exorcists fail because they invoke a power they do not belong to, and the spirit's question, "who are ye?", exposes the gulf between a borrowed formula and living faith.

Real repentance costs something visible. The Ephesians burn valuable books, so conversion means renouncing the practices and the profits that governed the old life rather than merely adding a new belief to them.

Opposition to the gospel is often economic before it is theological: Demetrius appeals to the honor of the goddess, but the grievance begins with threatened wealth, and religious fervor only supplies the riot its language.

crossRefs.label: Acts 8:14-17 — Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans, who receive the Holy Ghost
crossRefs.why: Samaritans who had already been "baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus" receive the Spirit only when apostles come down and lay hands on them. Read with Ephesus, the repetition shows a distinct apostolic gesture following baptism, which the Catholic tradition identifies as the root of confirmation.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:37-39 — repent and be baptized, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost
crossRefs.why: Peter promises that repentance and baptism bring "the gift of the Holy Ghost" to all whom the Lord shall call, naming no further rite. Protestant interpreters generally take this as the normal pattern and read the Samaritan and Ephesian episodes as extraordinary moments belonging to the gospel's spread into new groups.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 18:9-14 — divination, enchantment, and consulting familiar spirits forbidden
crossRefs.why: The law bans the whole apparatus of divination, enchantment, and necromancy that the Ephesian converts pile up and burn. The link presents their bonfire as obedience to an ancient command rather than as a novel Christian scruple invented on the spot.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 16:8-9 — a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries
crossRefs.why: Paul writes from this very city that "a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries." It is his own compressed summary of the chapter, holding the extraordinary fruitfulness and the riot together as one situation rather than as success followed by setback.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 6:10-18 — the whole armour of God against principalities and powers
crossRefs.why: Writing to this church, Paul insists that "we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers." Addressed to a congregation born amid exorcisms, burned magic books, and a riot for Diana, the imagery reads as pastoral realism rather than as decorative metaphor.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the sequence at Ephesus, baptism "in the name of the Lord Jesus" followed by Paul laying hands so that "the Holy Ghost came on them," is read as an apostolic instance of a rite distinct from baptism, the ancestor of confirmation, in which the Spirit is given through the ministry of those holding apostolic office.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the episode as transitional and exceptional: these men stood between the preparatory baptism of John and the Christian gospel, and God visibly joined them to the one Church through an apostle rather than instituting a permanent second rite. They usually hold that in the ordinary case the Spirit is given together with faith and baptism. Both traditions confess that the Spirit is God's own gift, that he is truly given to believers, and that no minister possesses him as property to dispense at will.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in the "handkerchiefs or aprons" carried from Paul's body to the sick a scriptural precedent for relics and sacramentals: because God has taken flesh, he freely chooses to work through material things associated with his saints, while the objects themselves possess no power of their own.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally treat these as "special miracles" that the text itself marks out as unusual, signs authenticating an apostle in a city saturated with magic, and they read the chapter's own contrast with the failed exorcists as a warning against handling holy things as instruments of power. Both traditions insist that God alone heals, that faith is directed to him rather than to any object, and that this same chapter condemns the manipulation of sacred names.

verses.text: And after the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples, and embraced them, and departed for to go into Macedonia.
And when he had gone over those parts, and had given them much exhortation, he came into Greece,
And there abode three months. And when the Jews laid wait for him, as he was about to sail into Syria, he purposed to return through Macedonia.
And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
These going before tarried for us at Troas.
And we sailed away from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread, and came unto them to Troas in five days; where we abode seven days.
And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
And there were many lights in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together.

And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead.
And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him.
When he therefore was come up again, and had broken bread, and eaten, and talked a long while, even till break of day, so he departed.
And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted.
And we went before to ship, and sailed unto Assos, there intending to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot.
And when he met with us at Assos, we took him in, and came to Mitylene.
And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail by Ephesus, because he would not spend the time in Asia: for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of Pentecost.
And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church.
And when they were come to him, he said unto them, Ye know, from the first day that I came into Asia, after what manner I have been with you at all seasons,
Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell me by the lying in wait of the Jews:
And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there:
Save that the Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions abide me.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
And now, behold, I know that ye all, among whom I have gone preaching the kingdom of God, shall see my face no more.
Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
I have coveted no man’s silver, or gold, or apparel.
Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.
I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
And when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all.
And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul’s neck, and kissed him,
Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him unto the ship.

chapters.summary: After the uproar Paul departs for Macedonia and Greece, where a plot forces him back overland. At Troas, "upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread," he preaches until midnight in the upper chamber; Eutychus, in a window, sinks into sleep and "fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead." Paul embraces him—"Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him"—then breaks bread and talks "even till break of day," and the young man is brought home alive. At Miletus he sends for "the elders of the church" at Ephesus and gives his one recorded address to pastors. He recalls serving "with all humility of mind, and with many tears," having "kept back nothing that was profitable" and taught "publickly, and from house to house." Now he goes "bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem," warned that "bonds and afflictions abide me," yet resolved to "finish my course with joy." Declaring himself "pure from the blood of all men" because he has "not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God," he charges them, "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood." He warns of "grievous wolves" from without and men who "arise, speaking perverse things" within, commends them to God, and cites the Lord: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." They kneel, weep, and walk him to the ship.
takeaways: The pastoral office is not self-chosen: "the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers," and its object is a flock God "hath purchased with his own blood," so authority in the Church is stewardship of what belongs to another at infinite cost.

Paul's model of teaching is exhaustive, "publickly, and from house to house," keeping back nothing profitable, which is why he can claim to be "pure from the blood of all men"; silence about hard doctrine is itself a failure of love.
The gravest dangers to a church come from within as much as from outside, since "grievous wolves" enter but men also rise up "of your own selves," making vigilance a permanent duty of those who lead.
The disciples gathering "upon the first day of the week" to break bread show the Christian Sunday assembly already formed, joining prolonged teaching and a shared table in a single act of worship.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 34:1-10 — woe to the shepherds of Israel that feed themselves
crossRefs.why: God indicts shepherds who "feed themselves" while the diseased, the broken, and the lost go unsought, and declares that he will require his flock at their hand. Paul's charge to the Ephesian elders is spoken directly out of this prophetic tradition of accountable shepherding.

crossRefs.label: John 10:11-16 — the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep
crossRefs.why: Jesus names himself the shepherd who lays down his life, unlike the hireling who abandons the sheep when the wolf comes. It stands behind Paul's language of a flock purchased with blood and of wolves the elders must not leave it to.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 5:1-4 — feed the flock of God, taking the oversight thereof
crossRefs.why: Peter charges elders to "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof," willingly rather than by constraint and "Neither as being lords over" those entrusted to them. The near-identical vocabulary shows a common apostolic understanding of the office rather than a view peculiar to Paul.

crossRefs.label: Titus 1:5-9 — ordain elders in every city, for a bishop must be blameless
crossRefs.why: Titus is told to "ordain elders in every city," and the qualifications that follow immediately speak of "a bishop," applying both words to the same men. Protestant interpreters generally read this beside Acts 20, where the elders are called overseers, as evidence that elder and bishop named one office in the apostolic churches.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 11:23-29 — the supper of the Lord handed on as what Paul received
crossRefs.why: Paul delivers "that which also I delivered unto you" concerning the bread and the cup, with the words "this is my body," and warns against receiving unworthily. Read with the Troas gathering, it fills in what breaking bread on the first day of the week meant in the churches Paul founded.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads Paul's charge, that "the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God," as the institution of a genuine pastoral office carrying divinely given responsibility to teach, govern, and sanctify, handed on from the apostles to the men they appointed, so the farewell at Miletus transfers care of the Ephesian church into their keeping.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally note that the same men are called elders and overseers within a single paragraph, and conclude that the apostolic churches knew a plurality of elders in each congregation rather than one bishop set above them, with an authority that is ministerial and always answerable to "the word of his grace" Paul commends them to. Both traditions affirm that the office is given by the Holy Spirit rather than seized, that pastors will answer for the flock, and that the Church belongs to the Christ who purchased it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread" as an early witness to the Sunday Eucharist: the assembly meets on the day of the resurrection, the word is preached at length, and the breaking of bread is the reason the community has gathered, which grounds the Church's understanding of Sunday worship as the ordinary shape of Christian life.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that the first day was already the settled day of assembly and that the breaking of bread here includes the Lord's Supper, though many read the phrase as also covering an ordinary shared meal and decline to derive a binding weekly obligation from a narrative detail. Both traditions agree that Christians met from the beginning on the first day of the week for teaching and the breaking of bread, and that the practice takes its meaning from the resurrection.

verses.text: And it came to pass, that after we were gotten from them, and had launched, we came with a straight course unto Coos, and the day following unto Rhodes, and from thence unto Patara:
And finding a ship sailing over unto Phenicia, we went aboard, and set forth.
Now when we had discovered Cyprus, we left it on the left hand, and sailed into Syria, and landed at Tyre: for there the ship was to unlade her burden.
And finding disciples, we tarried there seven days: who said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem.

And when we had accomplished those days, we departed and went our way; and they all brought us on our way, with wives and children, till we were out of the city: and we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed.
And when we had taken our leave one of another, we took ship; and they returned home again.
And when we had finished our course from Tyre, we came to Ptolemais, and saluted the brethren, and abode with them one day.
And the next day we that were of Paul’s company departed, and came unto Cæsarea: and we entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven; and abode with him.
And the same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.
And as we tarried there many days, there came down from Judæa a certain prophet, named Agabus.

And when he was come unto us, he took Paul’s girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.
And when we heard these things, both we, and they of that place, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done.
And after those days we took up our carriages, and went up to Jerusalem.
There went with us also certain of the disciples of Cæsarea, and brought with them one Mnason of Cyprus, an old disciple, with whom we should lodge.
And when we were come to Jerusalem, the brethren received us gladly.
And the day following Paul went in with us unto James; and all the elders were present.
And when he had saluted them, he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry.
And when they heard it, they glorified the Lord, and said unto him, Thou seest, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe; and they are all zealous of the law:

And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs.
What is it therefore? the multitude must needs come together: for they will hear that thou art come.
Do therefore this that we say to thee: We have four men which have a vow on them;

Them take, and purify thyself with them, and be at charges with them, that they may shave their heads: and all may know that those things, whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing; but that thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law.

As touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled, and from fornication.

Then Paul took the men, and the next day purifying himself with them entered into the temple, to signify the accomplishment of the days of purification, until that an offering should be offered for every one of them.
And when the seven days were almost ended, the Jews which were of Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the people, and laid hands on him,

Crying out, Men of Israel, help: This is the man, that teacheth all men every where against the people, and the law, and this place: and further brought Greeks also into the temple, and hath polluted this holy place.
( For they had seen before with him in the city Trophimus an Ephesian, whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple.)
And all the city was moved, and the people ran together: and they took Paul, and drew him out of the temple: and forthwith the doors were shut.
And as they went about to kill him, tidings came unto the chief captain of the band, that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
Who immediately took soldiers and centurions, and ran down unto them: and when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, they left beating of Paul.
Then the chief captain came near, and took him, and commanded him to be bound with two chains; and demanded who he was, and what he had done.
And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle.
And when he came upon the stairs, so it was, that he was borne of the soldiers for the violence of the people.
For the multitude of the people followed after, crying, Away with him.
And as Paul was to be led into the castle, he said unto the chief captain, May I speak unto thee? Who said, Canst thou speak Greek?
Art not thou that Egyptian, which before these days madest an uproar, and leddest out into the wilderness four thousand men that were murderers?
But Paul said, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city: and, I beseech thee, suffer me to speak unto the people.
And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,

chapters.summary: Sailing by Rhodes and Patara past Cyprus to Tyre, they find disciples who "said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem," then kneel with them on the shore to pray. At Caesarea they lodge with "Philip the evangelist," whose four daughters "did prophesy." The prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's girdle and declares, "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle." Begged to turn back, Paul answers, "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus," and the pleading ends, "The will of the Lord be done." To James and the elders he reports "what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry." They glorify God, then warn that believing Jews "are all zealous of the law" and have heard he teaches Jews "to forsake Moses." So Paul joins four men under a vow, paying their charges, that all may know the reports "are nothing" and he "walkest orderly, and keepest the law," while the ruling for Gentiles stands. Asian Jews seeing him in the temple cry, "Men of Israel, help," charging that he teaches "against the people, and the law, and this place." The mob drags him out; soldiers bind him with "two chains" as the crowd shouts, "Away with him"; from the stairs he speaks "in the Hebrew tongue."
takeaways: The Spirit's warning of suffering is not a command to avoid it. The disciples at Tyre and the sign of Agabus tell Paul truly what awaits him, yet the same Spirit is drawing him toward it, so discernment here means counting the cost rather than escaping it.

"The will of the Lord be done" is how a community stops arguing with God. Love that wants to shield someone from suffering is genuine, but it must finally yield to a vocation it did not choose and cannot control.

Unity in the Church is not uniformity of practice. Jewish believers keep the ancestral observances with apostolic approval while Gentile believers are not bound to them, and both belong to one body without either being made the condition of the other.
Acting prudently does not guarantee peace. Paul submits to the elders and performs a visibly pious act, and the riot happens anyway, which cautions against measuring faithfulness by its outcomes.

crossRefs.label: Acts 20:22-24 — Paul goes bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Speaking to the Ephesian elders, Paul says he goes "bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there," except that "bonds and afflictions abide me." It shows that the prophecies at Tyre and Caesarea confirm what Paul already expected rather than offering him a way out.

crossRefs.label: Acts 15:19-29 — the apostolic decree that Gentile believers are not bound to the law of Moses
crossRefs.why: The council at Jerusalem rules that Gentile converts should abstain only from "pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood." James restates that decision here in nearly identical words, showing that Paul's temple vow changes nothing about Gentile freedom.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 6:13-21 — the law of the Nazarite, the shaved head, and the required offering
crossRefs.why: The law prescribes that when the days of separation are fulfilled the Nazarite shall "shave the head of his separation" and bring an offering at the sanctuary. It explains what the four men were doing, what Paul paid for, and why the temple was the necessary setting for the episode that triggers his arrest.

crossRefs.label: Luke 22:39-46 — Gethsemane, and not my will, but thine, be done
crossRefs.why: In the garden Jesus kneels and prays, "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." The company's surrender, "The will of the Lord be done," sets Paul's road to Jerusalem inside the pattern of his Lord's own resolve, which the same author narrated in his Gospel.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 9:19-23 — unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews
crossRefs.why: Paul explains that he makes himself "servant unto all" and becomes "all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." Protestant interpreters generally read the purification in the temple through this principle, as missionary accommodation freely chosen rather than an obligation still binding on him.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Paul's acceptance of the elders' plan is read as a real act of obedience to the governing authority of the Church, and his purification in the temple as evidence that the gospel fulfills Israel's worship rather than abolishing it, so that Jewish believers could continue the ancestral observances without contradiction even though those observances were never imposed on Gentiles.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the episode as prudent accommodation in a matter left free, undertaken to defuse a false rumor rather than because the ceremonial law retained any binding force. Some add that the strategy visibly fails, which underlines that peace with the law was never the gospel's foundation. Both traditions agree that Paul never treats the vow as contributing to justification, and that the same chapter reaffirms Gentile believers are not placed under the law.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats Paul's answer, that he is "ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus," as the settled disposition of martyrdom, in which a believer freely offers his own suffering in union with Christ rather than merely enduring what cannot be avoided.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally emphasize that Paul's courage rests on God's sovereign purpose already declared over his life, so that his willingness to die is the confident response of a man who knows the outcome is held by God rather than an offering that adds anything to Christ's finished work. Both traditions agree that the Spirit's foretelling of his chains is meant to prepare him and the Church for suffering, not to redirect him away from it.
