verses.text: Men, brethren, and fathers, hear ye my defence which I make now unto you.
( And when they heard that he spake in the Hebrew tongue to them, they kept the more silence: and he saith,)

I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.
And I persecuted this way unto the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.

As also the high priest doth bear me witness, and all the estate of the elders: from whom also I received letters unto the brethren, and went to Damascus, to bring them which were there bound unto Jerusalem, for to be punished.
And it came to pass, that, as I made my journey, and was come nigh unto Damascus about noon, suddenly there shone from heaven a great light round about me.
And I fell unto the ground, and heard a voice saying unto me, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
And I answered, Who art thou, Lord? And he said unto me, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest.
And they that were with me saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they heard not the voice of him that spake to me.
And I said, What shall I do, Lord? And the Lord said unto me, Arise, and go into Damascus; and there it shall be told thee of all things which are appointed for thee to do.
And when I could not see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand of them that were with me, I came into Damascus.
And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there,
Came unto me, and stood, and said unto me, Brother Saul, receive thy sight. And the same hour I looked up upon him.
And he said, The God of our fathers hath chosen thee, that thou shouldest know his will, and see that Just One, and shouldest hear the voice of his mouth.
For thou shalt be his witness unto all men of what thou hast seen and heard.
And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord.
And it came to pass, that, when I was come again to Jerusalem, even while I prayed in the temple, I was in a trance;
And saw him saying unto me, Make haste, and get thee quickly out of Jerusalem: for they will not receive thy testimony concerning me.
And I said, Lord, they know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue them that believed on thee:
And when the blood of thy martyr Stephen was shed, I also was standing by, and consenting unto his death, and kept the raiment of them that slew him.
And he said unto me, Depart: for I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles.
And they gave him audience unto this word, and then lifted up their voices, and said, Away with such a fellow from the earth: for it is not fit that he should live.
And as they cried out, and cast off their clothes, and threw dust into the air,
The chief captain commanded him to be brought into the castle, and bade that he should be examined by scourging; that he might know wherefore they cried so against him.
And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?
When the centurion heard that, he went and told the chief captain, saying, Take heed what thou doest: for this man is a Roman.
Then the chief captain came, and said unto him, Tell me, art thou a Roman? He said, Yea.
And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born.
Then straightway they departed from him which should have examined him: and the chief captain also was afraid, after he knew that he was a Roman, and because he had bound him.

On the morrow, because he would have known the certainty wherefore he was accused of the Jews, he loosed him from his bands, and commanded the chief priests and all their council to appear, and brought Paul down, and set him before them.

chapters.summary: From the castle stairs Paul opens, "Men, brethren, and fathers, hear ye my defence which I make now unto you," and the crowd quiets at hearing "the Hebrew tongue." He begins with his standing among them: a Jew of Tarsus "brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel," and "zealous toward God, as ye all are this day." He admits he "persecuted this way unto the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women." Then the road: near Damascus "about noon" a great light throws him down and a voice asks, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" To his "Who art thou, Lord?" comes the answer, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest." Blinded, he is led in by hand, and Ananias, "a devout man according to the law," comes with "Brother Saul, receive thy sight," tells him "The God of our fathers hath chosen thee" to "see that Just One," and urges, "arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord." Praying later in the temple, he falls into "a trance," is told to leave Jerusalem, and protests his record at the death of "thy martyr Stephen," where he stood "consenting unto his death." The reply, "Depart: for I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles," breaks the silence: "Away with such a fellow from the earth." Ordered "examined by scourging," Paul asks whether it is lawful to scourge "a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned"; the frightened captain unbinds him and convenes the council.
takeaways: Christian testimony is not a claim to have been better than one's hearers. Paul builds his defense out of his own guilt, so the story he tells is about mercy overtaking a persecutor rather than about his own credentials.

The risen Christ identifies himself with those who are attacked: "why persecutest thou me?" makes injury done to the Church an injury done to him, which is the seed of the teaching that believers are members of his body.

Grace comes through a sent human being. God does not simply heal Saul directly; he sends Ananias with a word, a touch, and a command to be baptized, so the encounter is completed through the ministry of the Church.

Baptism is joined to the washing away of sins and to calling on the name of the Lord, which binds the outward rite, the inward cleansing, and the confession of faith into a single act rather than leaving them as separate stages.

crossRefs.label: Acts 9:1-19 — the road to Damascus told as narrative
crossRefs.why: The first account reports the same light, the same words "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" and Ananias restoring his sight, adding the Lord's word that he is "a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings." Reading it beside Paul's own retelling shows what he selects and stresses when speaking to a hostile Jerusalem crowd.

crossRefs.label: Acts 26:12-18 — the same call retold before King Agrippa
crossRefs.why: Before a Roman court Paul again describes the light and the voice, and this time the commission is spoken directly by Christ, to "open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light." The three tellings together show one event addressed to three audiences, each drawing out a different aspect of the same call.

crossRefs.label: Acts 7:54-60 — the stoning of Stephen, with Saul at the witnesses' feet
crossRefs.why: Stephen dies praying, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge," while the witnesses lay down their clothes at the feet of a young man "whose name was Saul." Paul's reference to "thy martyr Stephen" here shows he never stopped reckoning with that day, and it hints that the martyr's prayer was answered in the persecutor's own conversion.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:37-39 — repent, and be baptized every one of you for the remission of sins
crossRefs.why: At Pentecost the crowd asks what to do and is told to "be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins." In the Catholic tradition this is read together with Ananias saying "wash away thy sins," as two witnesses that baptism is the ordinary means by which God actually remits sin rather than a sign added afterward.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 1:11-17 — Paul insists his gospel came by revelation, not from man
crossRefs.why: Paul writes that he "neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ," and that after his call he "conferred not with flesh and blood." Protestant interpreters generally read this alongside the Damascus account as showing that his authority rests on Christ's direct commission, even though Acts records a human minister sent to him.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the command "arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins" is read as showing that baptism truly effects the forgiveness of sins rather than only picturing it, and that God chose to deliver that grace through a minister sent to Saul rather than in the vision on the road, which is taken as an early pattern of sacramental mediation within the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the phrase as vivid covenantal language for what baptism signifies and seals, holding that Saul's sins were forgiven when Christ met him and called him, with the washing publicly enacting a cleansing already granted through faith. Both traditions agree that the text refuses to separate baptism from conversion, and that Ananias is genuinely sent by God rather than acting on his own initiative.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the words "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" as revealing that Christ is so united to his Church that harm done to believers is suffered by him, which grounds the understanding of the Church as his body rather than as a voluntary association gathered around his memory.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally affirm the same union while locating it in the believer's spiritual incorporation into Christ by faith, so that the words express his covenantal solidarity with his people rather than an institutional identification with a visible body. Both traditions agree that the question makes persecution of Christians an offense against Christ himself, and that this is what turned Saul from a defender of God's honor into a servant of the one he was attacking.

verses.text: And Paul, earnestly beholding the council, said, Men and brethren, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day.
And the high priest Ananias commanded them that stood by him to smite him on the mouth.
Then said Paul unto him, God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law?
And they that stood by said, Revilest thou God’s high priest?
Then said Paul, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people.

But when Paul perceived that the one part were Sadducees, and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, Men and brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee: of the hope and resurrection of the dead I am called in question.
And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided.
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit: but the Pharisees confess both.

And there arose a great cry: and the scribes that were of the Pharisees’ part arose, and strove, saying, We find no evil in this man: but if a spirit or an angel hath spoken to him, let us not fight against God.

And when there arose a great dissension, the chief captain, fearing lest Paul should have been pulled in pieces of them, commanded the soldiers to go down, and to take him by force from among them, and to bring him into the castle.
And the night following the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome.
And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.
And they were more than forty which had made this conspiracy.
And they came to the chief priests and elders, and said, We have bound ourselves under a great curse, that we will eat nothing until we have slain Paul.

Now therefore ye with the council signify to the chief captain that he bring him down unto you to morrow, as though ye would enquire something more perfectly concerning him: and we, or ever he come near, are ready to kill him.
And when Paul’s sister’s son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul.
Then Paul called one of the centurions unto him, and said, Bring this young man unto the chief captain: for he hath a certain thing to tell him.
So he took him, and brought him to the chief captain, and said, Paul the prisoner called me unto him, and prayed me to bring this young man unto thee, who hath something to say unto thee.
Then the chief captain took him by the hand, and went with him aside privately, and asked him, What is that thou hast to tell me?
And he said, The Jews have agreed to desire thee that thou wouldest bring down Paul to morrow into the council, as though they would enquire somewhat of him more perfectly.

But do not thou yield unto them: for there lie in wait for him of them more than forty men, which have bound themselves with an oath, that they will neither eat nor drink till they have killed him: and now are they ready, looking for a promise from thee.
So the chief captain then let the young man depart, and charged him, See thou tell no man that thou hast shewed these things to me.
And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Cæsarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night;
And provide them beasts, that they may set Paul on, and bring him safe unto Felix the governor.
And he wrote a letter after this manner:
Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting.
This man was taken of the Jews, and should have been killed of them: then came I with an army, and rescued him, having understood that he was a Roman.
And when I would have known the cause wherefore they accused him, I brought him forth into their council:
Whom I perceived to be accused of questions of their law, but to have nothing laid to his charge worthy of death or of bonds.
And when it was told me how that the Jews laid wait for the man, I sent straightway to thee, and gave commandment to his accusers also to say before thee what they had against him. Farewell.
Then the soldiers, as it was commanded them, took Paul, and brought him by night to Antipatris.
On the morrow they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the castle:
Who, when they came to Cæsarea, and delivered the epistle to the governor, presented Paul also before him.
And when the governor had read the letter, he asked of what province he was. And when he understood that he was of Cilicia;
I will hear thee, said he, when thine accusers are also come. And he commanded him to be kept in Herod’s judgment hall.

chapters.summary: Paul opens before the council, "Men and brethren, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day," and the high priest Ananias orders him struck on the mouth. He answers, "God shall smite thee, thou whited wall," since a judge who commands a blow "contrary to the law" cannot judge by it; told whom he reviled, he withdraws at once, "I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest," citing the command against speaking "evil of the ruler of thy people." Seeing the chamber divided, he cries, "I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee: of the hope and resurrection of the dead I am called in question," and the hearing splits, since "the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit: but the Pharisees confess both." Scribes of the Pharisees concede, "We find no evil in this man," and the chief captain, fearing Paul will be "pulled in pieces," hauls him back to the castle. That night the Lord stands by him: "Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome." More than forty men bind themselves "under a curse" to eat nothing until Paul is dead, but his nephew warns the captain, who moves him to Caesarea by night under heavy guard. The letter from Claudius Lysias reports him "accused of questions of their law" yet with "nothing laid to his charge worthy of death." Felix holds him for trial when the accusers arrive.
takeaways: Paul appeals to a conscience clear "before God," not to a record clear before his accusers. Conscience in this sense is the interior court where a person answers to God, and it can acquit even when human tribunals condemn.

The quick retraction after his outburst matters as much as the outburst. He does not defend his anger; he corrects himself against the standard of Scripture, which is what a formed conscience looks like under pressure.
The resurrection is the true issue of the trial, not temple procedure. Paul names it because everything he preaches rests on it, so his defense is a confession rather than a courtroom tactic.

God's assurance comes as a commission, not as rescue from danger. "So must thou bear witness also at Rome" tells Paul he will survive because there is testimony still to give, which is how providence usually reaches those who suffer.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 22:28 — thou shalt not curse the ruler of thy people
crossRefs.why: The law forbids reviling and commands, "nor curse the ruler of thy people." Paul cites this command to retract his own sharp words, showing that he submits his conscience to Scripture even when he believes the officeholder has just acted lawlessly.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 22:23-33 — Jesus answers the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection
crossRefs.why: The Sadducees pose a riddle to discredit the resurrection and are told, "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God," since God "is not the God of the dead, but of the living." The exchange explains the fault line that splits the council here and shows Paul standing where his Master stood.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 15:12-20 — if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen
crossRefs.why: Paul argues that if the dead do not rise "then is Christ not risen" and "your faith is also vain," but insists that "now is Christ risen from the dead." It shows why he could tell the council that the resurrection was the whole question at issue rather than reducing the charge to a convenient party dispute.

crossRefs.label: Acts 27:21-25 — Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar
crossRefs.why: In the storm an angel repeats the same promise, "Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Cæsar," and Paul urges the crew to "be of good cheer" because "I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me." The later scene shows the night vision here holding firm through shipwreck, so the promise of Rome governs the rest of the book.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 1:18-19 — holding faith, and a good conscience
crossRefs.why: Timothy is charged to war a good warfare "Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck." Read with Paul's opening claim before the council, it treats a good conscience not as a feeling of innocence but as something a believer must actively keep, and whose loss endangers faith itself.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Paul's appeal to "all good conscience before God" and his immediate retraction when reminded of the law are read together as a portrait of a rightly formed conscience: an inward judgment that genuinely binds and must be followed, yet is never a law unto itself, since it is answerable to God's revealed word and can be corrected by it on the spot.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally place the emphasis on Scripture as the conscience's only sure captor, so that Paul's correction illustrates a conscience bound directly by the written word rather than by any further authority. Some also note that a clear conscience is not by itself proof of innocence, since Paul once persecuted the Church with a clear one. Both traditions agree that conscience must be obeyed and must also be formed, and that Scripture is what forms it here.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats Paul's declaration, "I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee: of the hope and resurrection of the dead I am called in question," as a truthful confession rather than a divisive maneuver, since it presents the gospel as the fulfillment of Israel's own hope, with the Church continuing rather than replacing the promise given to the fathers.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that the resurrection is the real charge, though some read the timing of the outburst as a deliberate and imperfect stratagem to fracture a hearing Paul judged to be rigged, and they stress that his hope is now defined by Christ risen rather than by his Pharisaic inheritance. Both traditions agree that the resurrection of the dead is the substance of the accusation against him and the reason the council could reach no verdict.

verses.text: And after five days Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and with a certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul.
And when he was called forth, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness, and that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence,
We accept it always, and in all places, most noble Felix, with all thankfulness.
Notwithstanding, that I be not further tedious unto thee, I pray thee that thou wouldest hear us of thy clemency a few words.
For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes:
Who also hath gone about to profane the temple: whom we took, and would have judged according to our law.
But the chief captain Lysias came upon us, and with great violence took him away out of our hands,
Commanding his accusers to come unto thee: by examining of whom thyself mayest take knowledge of all these things, whereof we accuse him.
And the Jews also assented, saying that these things were so.

Then Paul, after that the governor had beckoned unto him to speak, answered, Forasmuch as I know that thou hast been of many years a judge unto this nation, I do the more cheerfully answer for myself:
Because that thou mayest understand, that there are yet but twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem for to worship.
And they neither found me in the temple disputing with any man, neither raising up the people, neither in the synagogues, nor in the city:
Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me.
But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:
And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.
Now after many years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings.
Whereupon certain Jews from Asia found me purified in the temple, neither with multitude, nor with tumult.
Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me.
Or else let these same here say, if they have found any evil doing in me, while I stood before the council,
Except it be for this one voice, that I cried standing among them, Touching the resurrection of the dead I am called in question by you this day.
And when Felix heard these things, having more perfect knowledge of that way, he deferred them, and said, When Lysias the chief captain shall come down, I will know the uttermost of your matter.
And he commanded a centurion to keep Paul, and to let him have liberty, and that he should forbid none of his acquaintance to minister or come unto him.
And after certain days, when Felix came with his wife Drusilla, which was a Jewess, he sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ.
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
He hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him: wherefore he sent for him the oftener, and communed with him.
But after two years Porcius Festus came into Felix’ room: and Felix, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound.

chapters.summary: After five days the high priest Ananias comes to Caesarea with elders and "a certain orator named Tertullus," who flatters Felix for the "great quietness" of his rule before charging that Paul is "a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition" and "a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes" who "hath gone about to profane the temple." Paul answers "more cheerfully," factual first: only "twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem for to worship," and "Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me." Then it turns to confession: "after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers," believing what is "written in the law and in the prophets," holding a hope his accusers share, "that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust," and therefore laboring "to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men." He came bringing "alms to my nation, and offerings," and was found "purified in the temple" by accusers now absent, "Who ought to have been here before thee." His one offense: the cry, "Touching the resurrection of the dead I am called in question." Felix, having "more perfect knowledge of that way," adjourns, grants Paul "liberty," and later hears him with Drusilla "concerning the faith in Christ." When Paul reasons "of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled" and postponed him to "a convenient season," hoping for a bribe; two years on, Festus succeeds him and Felix leaves Paul bound.
takeaways: Truth can be accused in polished language and defended in plain speech. Tertullus opens with flattery and sweeping labels, while Paul answers with dates, places, and the observation that nothing charged can be proved.

Paul does not defend himself by minimizing his faith. He concedes the name his accusers use for it and then confesses the whole of it, showing that an honest defense may concede facts but never the substance of belief.

The resurrection of "both of the just and unjust" means every life is finally accountable, which is why Paul says it produces the daily discipline of keeping a conscience free of offense toward God and toward neighbor alike.

Felix trembling and then deferring is one of Scripture's sharpest pictures of grace resisted. Conviction is real, the moment is genuine, and it is still possible to postpone conversion to a season that never comes.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 12:1-3 — many that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake
crossRefs.why: The prophet foretells that "many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." It is the clearest place in the prophets for the twofold resurrection Paul says his accusers "themselves also allow," which shows his hope is not a novelty but Israel's own written expectation.

crossRefs.label: John 5:28-29 — the resurrection of life and the resurrection of damnation
crossRefs.why: Jesus says all in the graves will hear his voice and come forth, "they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation." In the Catholic tradition this is read with Paul's twofold resurrection as evidence that the deeds of a life genuinely enter into the final judgment, which is why he speaks of exercising himself to keep a clear conscience.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 9:27-28 — it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment
crossRefs.why: The letter states plainly that death is followed by judgment, and that to "them that look for him" Christ will "appear the second time without sin unto salvation." It supplies the doctrine behind the "judgment to come" that made Felix tremble, and shows that the warning was not a threat invented for the occasion.

crossRefs.label: Romans 15:25-31 — the collection carried to the poor saints at Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Paul writes that he goes to Jerusalem "to minister unto the saints," carrying "a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem," and asks prayer that he be delivered from those who do not believe there. It identifies the "alms to my nation, and offerings" mentioned only in passing here, and shows he foresaw the very danger this trial arose from.

crossRefs.label: Acts 21:26-29 — Paul purifying himself in the temple, and the charge about Trophimus
crossRefs.why: The narrative records that Paul entered the temple "purifying himself" with the four men, and that the accusation of bringing Greeks in rested on a supposition about Trophimus. Reading it behind Tertullus' charge of profaning the temple lets the reader see exactly where the accusation departs from what happened.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Paul's pairing of "a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust" with his effort "to have always a conscience void of offence" is read as showing that the coming judgment takes real account of how a life has been lived, so that grace works itself out in deeds that will be weighed, and moral effort is part of salvation rather than a threat to it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally hold that the believer's standing at that judgment rests on Christ's righteousness received by faith, with a clear conscience and good works serving as the evidence and fruit of that faith rather than as its ground. They note that Paul elsewhere insists no one is justified by the works of the law. Both traditions agree that the final judgment is real, that it takes the whole of a life into account, and that the Christian is called to a conscience free of offense before God and neighbor.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in Felix, who "trembled" and then answered "Go thy way for this time," a warning about human freedom before grace: the conviction was genuine and sufficient, yet grace can be truly offered and truly deferred, and the convenient season he waited for never comes in the narrative.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read Felix as an example of conviction without conversion, the kind of alarm the conscience can feel under preaching while the will remains unchanged, and many stress that only God's effective work turns such trembling into faith. They also note the text names his real motive, that "he hoped also that money should have been given him." Both traditions agree that hearing the word and being shaken by it is not the same as repenting, and that delay in this chapter hardens into two years of leaving Paul bound.

verses.text: Now when Festus was come into the province, after three days he ascended from Cæsarea to Jerusalem.
Then the high priest and the chief of the Jews informed him against Paul, and besought him,
And desired favour against him, that he would send for him to Jerusalem, laying wait in the way to kill him.
But Festus answered, that Paul should be kept at Cæsarea, and that he himself would depart shortly thither.
Let them therefore, said he, which among you are able, go down with me, and accuse this man, if there be any wickedness in him.
And when he had tarried among them more than ten days, he went down unto Cæsarea; and the next day sitting on the judgment seat commanded Paul to be brought.
And when he was come, the Jews which came down from Jerusalem stood round about, and laid many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove.
While he answered for himself, Neither against the law of the Jews, neither against the temple, nor yet against Cæsar, have I offended any thing at all.
But Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure, answered Paul, and said, Wilt thou go up to Jerusalem, and there be judged of these things before me?
Then said Paul, I stand at Cæsar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest.

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Cæsar.
Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, Hast thou appealed unto Cæsar? unto Cæsar shalt thou go.
And after certain days king Agrippa and Bernice came unto Cæsarea to salute Festus.
And when they had been there many days, Festus declared Paul’s cause unto the king, saying, There is a certain man left in bonds by Felix:
About whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, desiring to have judgment against him.

To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him.
Therefore, when they were come hither, without any delay on the morrow I sat on the judgment seat, and commanded the man to be brought forth.
Against whom when the accusers stood up, they brought none accusation of such things as I supposed:
But had certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
And because I doubted of such manner of questions, I asked him whether he would go to Jerusalem, and there be judged of these matters.
But when Paul had appealed to be reserved unto the hearing of Augustus, I commanded him to be kept till I might send him to Cæsar.
Then Agrippa said unto Festus, I would also hear the man myself. To morrow, said he, thou shalt hear him.

And on the morrow, when Agrippa was come, and Bernice, with great pomp, and was entered into the place of hearing, with the chief captains, and principal men of the city, at Festus’ commandment Paul was brought forth.

And Festus said, King Agrippa, and all men which are here present with us, ye see this man, about whom all the multitude of the Jews have dealt with me, both at Jerusalem, and also here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
But when I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and that he himself hath appealed to Augustus, I have determined to send him.

Of whom I have no certain thing to write unto my lord. Wherefore I have brought him forth before you, and specially before thee, O king Agrippa, that, after examination had, I might have somewhat to write.
For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him.

chapters.summary: When Festus is "come into the province," he goes up to Jerusalem, where the high priest and the chief of the Jews inform him against Paul and "desired favour against him," asking that he be summoned while men are "laying wait in the way to kill him." Festus keeps him at Caesarea and bids them come down and "accuse this man, if there be any wickedness in him." On the judgment seat he hears "many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove," while Paul answers that he has offended "Neither against the law of the Jews, neither against the temple, nor yet against Cæsar." Festus, "willing to do the Jews a pleasure," proposes a trial at Jerusalem; Paul refuses the trap and stands on his citizenship, "I stand at Cæsar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged," and "I appeal unto Cæsar." Festus confers and answers, "Hast thou appealed unto Cæsar? unto Cæsar shalt thou go." King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus lays out the case, insisting it is "not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die" before the accused meets "the accusers face to face," and admitting the dispute turns on "one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Agrippa says, "I would also hear the man myself." The next day, amid "great pomp," before chief captains and principal men, Paul is brought forth; Festus grants he has "committed nothing worthy of death," yet confesses, "I have no certain thing to write unto my lord."
takeaways: Paul's appeal to Caesar shows that claiming the protection of just civil law is compatible with trust in God; grace does not require a believer to surrender legitimate rights or to court an unjust death.

Roman procedure insists that an accused man meet "the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself," and the chapter quietly commends that due process as a real good even when the officials administering it are self-interested.

Festus reduces the whole matter to "certain questions" about "one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Worldly power can register the resurrection as a procedural nuisance and still miss that everything hangs on whether the claim is true.

God's purposes advance through unremarkable machinery: a governor's ambition, a change of jurisdiction, a legal appeal. Providence is not only in the dramatic vision but in the delay, the paperwork, and the escort.

crossRefs.label: Acts 23:11 — so must thou bear witness also at Rome
crossRefs.why: The Lord stands by Paul in Jerusalem and promises that as he has testified there, "so must thou bear witness also at Rome." Read alongside chapter 25, the appeal to Caesar becomes the visible means by which that promise is kept.

crossRefs.label: Acts 9:15-16 — a chosen vessel to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings
crossRefs.why: At Paul's calling the Lord says he will carry the name "before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel," and will be shown "how great things he must suffer." The hearing before Festus and Agrippa is that commission arriving in its literal form, suffering and royal audience together.

crossRefs.label: Luke 21:12-15 — brought before kings and rulers, and it shall turn to you for a testimony
crossRefs.why: Jesus forewarns that his disciples will be delivered to prisons and "brought before kings and rulers for my name’s sake," and that the occasion "shall turn to you for a testimony" with a God-given mouth and wisdom. Acts 25 stages exactly that scene, so the trial reads as opportunity rather than mere misfortune.

crossRefs.label: Romans 13:1-4 — the powers that be are ordained of God
crossRefs.why: Paul teaches that civil authority is God's minister for good and is to be honored rather than despised. That the same apostle submits to a Roman court and invokes its protection shows the teaching lived out, and it frames Festus's flawed magistracy as still a genuine instrument of order.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 50:19-20 — ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good
crossRefs.why: Joseph interprets a conspiracy against him as something God bent toward saving "much people alive." The plot to ambush Paul on the Jerusalem road, and the political calculation that follows it, work the same way: hostile intent becomes the road by which God's servant reaches the place appointed for him.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Paul's conduct here is read as a model of the right relation between the Church and lawful civil authority: the state possesses a real, God-given competence in matters of justice and public order, so a Christian may rightly submit to its courts, cooperate with its procedures, and claim its protections without compromising fidelity to Christ.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the scene the same way but press harder on the limits: Festus is "willing to do the Jews a pleasure," so the passage also exposes how easily magistrates bend justice, and Paul's appeal is treated as prudent use of a flawed system rather than any endorsement of Rome. Both traditions affirm that civil government is ordained by God for justice, that its authority is real but derived and answerable, and that obedience to it never overrides obedience to God.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to this chapter as a portrait of providence working through secondary causes: God's declared purpose that Paul reach Rome is accomplished not by suspending events but through a governor's ambition, a prisoner's own deliberate act of appeal, and the ordinary grinding of Roman law, so that the human choices are genuinely free and genuinely the means.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally frame the same events under God's sovereign decree, holding that the outcome was certain and that Paul's appeal was the appointed instrument rather than an independent contribution to it. Some also debate whether the appeal showed faith or impatience, though most read it as sober wisdom in the face of a planned ambush. Both traditions agree that the chapter's quiet, unmiraculous machinery is exactly where God is at work, and that trusting his promise does not make human decision unnecessary.

verses.text: Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Thou art permitted to speak for thyself. Then Paul stretched forth the hand, and answered for himself:
I think myself happy, king Agrippa, because I shall answer for myself this day before thee touching all the things whereof I am accused of the Jews:
Especially because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews: wherefore I beseech thee to hear me patiently.
My manner of life from my youth, which was at the first among mine own nation at Jerusalem, know all the Jews;
Which knew me from the beginning, if they would testify, that after the most straitest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
And now I stand and am judged for the hope of the promise made of God unto our fathers:
Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come. For which hope’s sake, king Agrippa, I am accused of the Jews.
Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead?
I verily thought with myself, that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
Which thing I also did in Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death, I gave my voice against them.
And I punished them oft in every synagogue, and compelled them to blaspheme; and being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto strange cities.
Whereupon as I went to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
At midday, O king, I saw in the way a light from heaven, above the brightness of the sun, shining round about me and them which journeyed with me.
And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
And I said, Who art thou, Lord? And he said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.

But rise, and stand upon thy feet: for I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness both of these things which thou hast seen, and of those things in the which I will appear unto thee;
Delivering thee from the people, and from the Gentiles, unto whom now I send thee,

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
Whereupon, O king Agrippa, I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision:
But shewed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judæa, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance.
For these causes the Jews caught me in the temple, and went about to kill me.
Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come:
That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles.
And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.
For the king knoweth of these things, before whom also I speak freely: for I am persuaded that none of these things are hidden from him; for this thing was not done in a corner.
King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest.
Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.
And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.
And when he had thus spoken, the king rose up, and the governor, and Bernice, and they that sat with them:
And when they were gone aside, they talked between themselves, saying, This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds.
Then said Agrippa unto Festus, This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Cæsar.

chapters.summary: Agrippa grants leave, "Thou art permitted to speak for thyself," and Paul "stretched forth the hand." He counts himself "happy" to plead before a king "expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews," and reframes the charge as a matter of hope: he stands "judged for the hope of the promise made of God unto our fathers," the hope toward which "our twelve tribes" serve "day and night." He puts the real question: "Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead?" Then he tells his own history, how he "verily thought" he "ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth," shutting saints in prison and being "exceedingly mad against them." On the Damascus road "At midday" a light "above the brightness of the sun" throws them all down, and a voice in "the Hebrew tongue" asks, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" and answers, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." He is made "a minister and a witness," sent "To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light." Paul answers, "I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision," and claims to preach nothing beyond what "the prophets and Moses did say should come." Festus cries that "much learning doth make thee mad"; Agrippa says, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." Paul wishes all present were as he is, "except these bonds"; the court withdraws agreeing he does "nothing worthy of death."
takeaways: Grace here is entirely unearned and unlooked-for: Christ confronts a man in the act of persecuting him, so the initiative belongs wholly to God, yet Paul summarizes his whole life afterward as a response — "I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision."

Paul presents the gospel as the fulfillment of Israel's hope rather than a departure from it, standing trial "for the hope of the promise made of God unto our fathers" and insisting the resurrection is what the prophets and Moses had said would come.

The commission maps the whole shape of conversion: eyes opened, a turn "from darkness to light," release "from the power of Satan unto God," forgiveness of sins, and "inheritance among them which are sanctified."

Agrippa's "Almost" is the chapter's warning — real interest that stops short of surrender — while Paul's wish that his judges were as he is "except these bonds" shows a charity toward them untouched by his own chains.

crossRefs.label: Acts 9:3-6 — the light from heaven and the voice on the Damascus road
crossRefs.why: Luke's own narration of the conversion records the same light, the same question, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" and the same self-naming of Jesus. Reading it beside chapter 26 shows what Paul adds when he testifies in his own voice before a king: the commission to the Gentiles is spoken directly on the road.

crossRefs.label: Acts 22:6-15 — Paul retells his conversion to the crowd in Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Speaking to a hostile Jewish crowd, Paul stresses that "The God of our fathers hath chosen thee" and that he is to be a witness "unto all men." Set beside the version given to Agrippa, the two show one apostle shaping the same testimony for two audiences without altering its substance.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 42:6-7 — a light of the Gentiles, to open the blind eyes and bring out the prisoners
crossRefs.why: The servant is given "for a light of the Gentiles," commissioned "To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness." Paul's account of his own sending borrows that vocabulary almost whole, presenting his mission as the servant's work being carried outward through him.

crossRefs.label: Luke 24:44-47 — thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day
crossRefs.why: The risen Jesus explains that all things written "in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms" concern him, and that repentance and remission are to be preached "among all nations." Paul's claim before Agrippa that he says only what "the prophets and Moses did say should come" is that lesson repeated under oath.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 1:12-16 — a blasphemer and a persecutor, who obtained mercy
crossRefs.why: Looking back, Paul calls himself the chief of sinners, saved so that Christ might "shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe." Protestant interpreters often read the Agrippa speech through this later reflection, as the clearest case that salvation is sheer unmerited mercy received by faith rather than anything the convert brought.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Paul's summary, "I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision," is read as showing that grace which is wholly gratuitous still calls for and enables a genuinely free human response, so that his lifelong obedience is truly his own act while being entirely the work of grace within him.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally stress that the encounter is unilateral, since Paul is struck down in the middle of persecuting the Church and contributes nothing to it, and they read his subsequent obedience as the fruit and evidence of a grace that effectually turns the will rather than a cooperating factor alongside it. Both traditions affirm that the initiative is entirely God's, that no merit of Paul's occasioned it, and that a grace which produced no obedience would not be the grace Paul describes.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the terms of the commission itself, that hearers "should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance," understanding conversion as a single movement completed in a changed life, so that charity in action belongs to the reality of turning to God and not merely to its aftermath.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the works as the necessary evidence of a repentance that itself receives forgiveness by faith, and they point to Paul's own summary placing "forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified" under "faith that is in me." Both traditions agree that repentance producing no changed conduct is not the repentance Paul preached, and that the forgiveness he announces is God's gift rather than a wage.

verses.text: And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus’ band.
And entering into a ship of Adramyttium, we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia; one Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.
And the next day we touched at Sidon. And Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself.
And when we had launched from thence, we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
And when we had sailed over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
And there the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy; and he put us therein.
And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone;
And, hardly passing it, came unto a place which is called The fair havens; nigh whereunto was the city of Lasea.
Now when much time was spent, and when sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was now already past, Paul admonished them,
And said unto them, Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives.
Nevertheless the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul.

And because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence also, if by any means they might attain to Phenice, and there to winter; which is an haven of Crete, and lieth toward the south west and north west.
And when the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, loosing thence, they sailed close by Crete.
But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon.
And when the ship was caught, and could not bear up into the wind, we let her drive.
And running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat:
Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven.
And we being exceedingly tossed with a tempest, the next day they lightened the ship;
And the third day we cast out with our own hands the tackling of the ship.
And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away.
But after long abstinence Paul stood forth in the midst of them, and said, Sirs, ye should have hearkened unto me, and not have loosed from Crete, and to have gained this harm and loss.
And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man’s life among you, but of the ship.
For there stood by me this night the angel of God, whose I am, and whom I serve,
Saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Cæsar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.
Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.
Howbeit we must be cast upon a certain island.
But when the fourteenth night was come, as we were driven up and down in Adria, about midnight the shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country;
And sounded, and found it twenty fathoms: and when they had gone a little further, they sounded again, and found it fifteen fathoms.
Then fearing lest we should have fallen upon rocks, they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day.
And as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship, when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off.
And while the day was coming on, Paul besought them all to take meat, saying, This day is the fourteenth day that ye have tarried and continued fasting, having taken nothing.
Wherefore I pray you to take some meat: for this is for your health: for there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you.
And when he had thus spoken, he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat.
Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat.
And we were in all in the ship two hundred threescore and sixteen souls.
And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, and cast out the wheat into the sea.
And when it was day, they knew not the land: but they discovered a certain creek with a shore, into the which they were minded, if it were possible, to thrust in the ship.
And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore.
And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
And the soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, lest any of them should swim out, and escape.
But the centurion, willing to save Paul, kept them from their purpose; and commanded that they which could swim should cast themselves first into the sea, and get to land:
And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land.

chapters.summary: Paul and other prisoners are delivered "unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus’ band" for the voyage to Italy. At Sidon Julius "courteously entreated Paul"; contrary winds drive them to Myra, where they transfer to "a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy." Having "sailed slowly many days," they barely reach The fair havens, and since "sailing was now dangerous," Paul warns that "this voyage will be with hurt and much damage." But "the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship," and the majority vote to press on. A soft south wind flatters them until "a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon" seizes the vessel; they undergird the hull and cast out the tackling, and when "neither sun nor stars in many days appeared," "all hope that we should be saved was then taken away." Paul stands forth with a word from the angel of God, "whose I am, and whom I serve": "Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Cæsar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee." He adds, "I believe God." Yet when the sailors try to slip off in the boat he tells the centurion, "Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved." At daybreak he urges them to eat, promising "there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you," then "took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all." All two hundred seventy-six aboard are cheered; the ship runs aground and breaks apart, and "they escaped all safe to land."
takeaways: The promise that no life would be lost did not make seamanship optional. "Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved" shows that a guaranteed end is reached through human means rather than around them, and that trusting a promise is not the same as doing nothing.

Paul's courage rests on a specific word received and believed — "I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me" — which is faith as trust in what has actually been said, not a general hopefulness about outcomes.

In the storm authority quietly passes from the owner and the centurion to the prisoner, because the man who says "whose I am, and whom I serve" is the only one on board with something steady to stand on. The whole company is spared in his company.
Giving thanks publicly in the middle of despair is itself an act of faith: the others become "of good cheer" and eat only after someone has broken bread and blessed God in front of them.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 107:23-30 — they that go down to the sea in ships see the wonders of the LORD in the deep
crossRefs.why: The psalm describes sailors driven to their wits' end by a storm God himself raised, who cry out and are brought "unto their desired haven." It supplies the scriptural pattern behind Luke's account, where the sea is not chaos outside God's reach but a place where his works are seen.

crossRefs.label: Jonah 1:4-16 — a tempest at sea, a lightened ship, and mariners who come to fear the LORD
crossRefs.why: Jonah's crew jettison cargo, plead with a God not their own, and end up worshipping him. The parallels with Acts 27 are close enough to sharpen the contrast: Jonah's presence endangers the ship, while Paul's presence is the reason God gives him "all them that sail with thee."

crossRefs.label: Luke 22:19 — he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it
crossRefs.why: At the supper Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, and breaks it with words of self-gift. Luke uses that same sequence for Paul in the storm, which is why the Catholic tradition hears a deliberate liturgical echo in a meal that turns terror into cheer.

crossRefs.label: Luke 21:16-19 — there shall not an hair of your head perish
crossRefs.why: Jesus promises his disciples ultimate preservation in the very sentence that warns some of them will be killed, so the promise plainly concerns something deeper than bodily safety. Paul's assurance that "there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you" borrows that language and applies it to a night when the ship itself is lost.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 2:12-13 — work out your own salvation, for it is God which worketh in you
crossRefs.why: Paul holds together strenuous human effort and God's inward working as one reality rather than two competing causes. That is precisely the logic of the shipwreck, where God's pledge that all will live stands alongside the order that the sailors must stay aboard.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition this chapter is a favored illustration of providence working through secondary causes: God's promise that he "hath given thee all them that sail with thee" is absolutely certain, and yet Paul must still say "Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved," so that free human acts are neither bypassed nor made pointless by the divine decree. The tradition has also read the ship as an image of the Church, the company being kept safe together rather than each man saving himself.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally reach the same practical conclusion by a different route, holding that God ordains the means along with the end, so that the sailors staying aboard was itself decreed rather than an independent condition God had to accommodate. They tend to resist pressing the ship into an allegory of the Church, reading it as a historical vessel in a historical storm. Both traditions agree that a sure promise never licenses passivity, and that the chapter forbids setting divine sovereignty and human responsibility against each other.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears a eucharistic resonance in Paul taking bread, giving "thanks to God in presence of them all," breaking it and eating, since Luke uses the same sequence of actions he uses for the Lord's supper and for the Emmaus meal, and since the act openly and publicly restores a despairing company.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read this as an ordinary meal opened with the customary Jewish blessing over food, noting that the two hundred and seventy-six aboard were soldiers, sailors, and prisoners rather than a believing congregation, and that no words of institution are recorded. Both traditions agree the gesture is deliberate and unmistakably Christian, a public act of thanksgiving that gives the whole ship courage before the wreck.

verses.text: And when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita.
And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
And when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks, and laid them on the fire, there came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.

And when the barbarians saw the venomous beast hang on his hand, they said among themselves, No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live.
And he shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm.

Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
In the same quarters were possessions of the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius; who received us, and lodged us three days courteously.
And it came to pass, that the father of Publius lay sick of a fever and of a bloody flux: to whom Paul entered in, and prayed, and laid his hands on him, and healed him.
So when this was done, others also, which had diseases in the island, came, and were healed:
Who also honoured us with many honours; and when we departed, they laded us with such things as were necessary.
And after three months we departed in a ship of Alexandria, which had wintered in the isle, whose sign was Castor and Pollux.
And landing at Syracuse, we tarried there three days.
And from thence we fetched a compass, and came to Rhegium: and after one day the south wind blew, and we came the next day to Puteoli:
Where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome.
And from thence, when the brethren heard of us, they came to meet us as far as Appii forum, and The three taverns: whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage.
And when we came to Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard: but Paul was suffered to dwell by himself with a soldier that kept him.

And it came to pass, that after three days Paul called the chief of the Jews together: and when they were come together, he said unto them, Men and brethren, though I have committed nothing against the people, or customs of our fathers, yet was I delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
Who, when they had examined me, would have let me go, because there was no cause of death in me.
But when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Cæsar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of.
For this cause therefore have I called for you, to see you, and to speak with you: because that for the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.
And they said unto him, We neither received letters out of Judæa concerning thee, neither any of the brethren that came shewed or spake any harm of thee.
But we desire to hear of thee what thou thinkest: for as concerning this sect, we know that every where it is spoken against.

And when they had appointed him a day, there came many to him into his lodging; to whom he expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening.
And some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not.
And when they agreed not among themselves, they departed, after that Paul had spoken one word, Well spake the Holy Ghost by Esaias the prophet unto our fathers,
Saying, Go unto this people, and say, Hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing ye shall see, and not perceive:

For the heart of this people is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes have they closed; lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.
Be it known therefore unto you, that the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles, and that they will hear it.
And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves.
And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,
Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.

chapters.summary: Ashore, they learn the island is "called Melita," where "the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness," kindling a fire against the rain and cold. A viper driven from the heat fastens on Paul's hand, and the islanders judge him "a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live." He shakes it into the fire and "felt no harm"; when he neither swells nor dies, "they changed their minds, and said that he was a god." Paul heals the fevered father of Publius, and other sick islanders are healed. After three months they sail in a ship "whose sign was Castor and Pollux" to Puteoli, where brethren receive them; met at "Appii forum, and The three taverns," Paul "thanked God, and took courage." At Rome he may "dwell by himself with a soldier that kept him." He summons the chief of the Jews and explains he wears his chain "for the hope of Israel"; they have had no letters against him but wish to hear him, since of "this sect" they know "every where it is spoken against." All day he expounds the kingdom of God "both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets," and "some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not." As they part he speaks the prophet's word about a "heart" that "is waxed gross," and declares "the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles." Luke closes with two years in a hired house, "Preaching the kingdom of God," "no man forbidding him."
takeaways: The viper and the healings are real signs, yet Luke lets the islanders swing from calling Paul a murderer to calling him "a god" without a word of faith between the two, a quiet caution that wonders impress but do not by themselves convert.

Paul insists the gospel is "the hope of Israel" rather than a rival to it, and he says he came to Rome "not that I had ought to accuse my nation of." The turn to the Gentiles is presented as the promise widening, not the promise withdrawn.

The prophetic word Paul quotes is a summons spoken within Israel by a Jewish apostle to his own people, the same word given long before to the prophet and repeated by Jesus to the crowds. It warns any hearer in any generation against eyes deliberately closed.

Acts ends with no verdict, no martyrdom, no tidy close. Its last note is "no man forbidding him," locating the book's real subject in the unhindered freedom of the word rather than in the fate of the apostle carrying it.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 6:9-10 — Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not
crossRefs.why: This is the passage Paul quotes as the last word of his Roman hearing, given to Isaiah at his own commissioning as a warning that his preaching would meet closed eyes. Read together, it shows Paul placing himself in the long line of prophets sent to their own people with a word both merciful and hard.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 13:14-15 — this people’s heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing
crossRefs.why: Jesus applies the same Isaiah oracle to the crowds who hear his parables without receiving them. That the identical text is used by the Lord and then by his apostle marks the division as one that runs through hearing itself, and one Jesus met first.

crossRefs.label: Romans 11:25-32 — the gifts and calling of God are without repentance
crossRefs.why: Writing to the very city he now reaches in chains, Paul teaches that Israel's partial blindness is temporary and purposeful, that its people remain "beloved for the fathers’ sakes," and that God has shut all up in unbelief "that he might have mercy upon all." It is the indispensable commentary on Acts 28, forbidding any reading of the closing scene as a final rejection.

crossRefs.label: Mark 16:17-18 — they shall take up serpents, and they shall lay hands on the sick
crossRefs.why: The risen Christ promises that signs will accompany those who believe, naming both immunity from serpents and healing by the laying on of hands. Acts 28 records both on a single island within a few verses, presenting the Melita episode as that promise verified rather than as a display Paul sought.

crossRefs.label: Romans 1:8-16 — I am ready to preach the gospel to you that are at Rome also
crossRefs.why: Years earlier Paul had written of his longing to come to Rome and of a gospel that is God's power to salvation "to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Acts 28 shows the longing answered in a way he had not imagined, under guard, and the order of that preaching kept exactly.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Paul's closing declaration that "the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles" is read as the widening of one covenant history rather than the cancelling of it: the same apostle who speaks the hard prophetic word is a Jew addressing his own people, wearing a chain "for the hope of Israel," and the tradition holds that God's election of Israel is never revoked.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that the mission moves outward here in fulfillment of the prophets rather than as a repudiation, though some place more weight on the note of division in "some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not," reading the Church as the community of faith gathered from Jew and Gentile alike. Both traditions affirm that the gospel is offered first within Israel, that the prophetic warning is a call to repentance and not a verdict on a people, and that the turn to the Gentiles fulfils what Israel's Scriptures had promised.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats the abrupt ending — two years of teaching "with all confidence, no man forbidding him," and no report of the trial's outcome — as deliberate rather than accidental, since Luke's subject is the progress of the word and the life of the apostolic community, which continues past the last page in the Church Paul left behind.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the ending the same way as a literary and theological choice, while many also find in it a historical clue that Luke wrote before the case was decided. They tend to locate the book's climax in the free proclamation itself, since the final words describe the word's liberty rather than the preacher's. Both traditions agree that Acts closes forward-looking, handing the mission on rather than concluding it.
